Discussion The results clearly show striking diel vertical migrations of T. extensus and P. remata over two consecutive days in Johnson Pond (Fig. 3). Tropocyclops displays a typical migration, avoiding the surface and occurring at greatest abundance near the bottom during the day. Polyarthra, on the other hand, exhibits a reverse migration, avoiding the bottom and moving to the surface during the day. The results of these two migrations is a marked spatial segregation of the two species during the day (Fig. 4). Typical diel migrations, such as that of T. extensus, are exhibited by a variety of freshwater zooplankton, and have been particularly well analysed in Daphnia, copepods and Chaoborus larvae (Hutchinson, 1967; Lampert & Sommer, 1997). These migrations with a diurnal descent increase fitness by decreasing encounters with visually feeding predators, notably fish, during the day, and they can be rapidly induced by the presence of the predator, or a kairomone released by the predator (Lampert, 1993; Lampert & Sommer, 1997; De Meester et al., 1999). While there are no fish in Johnson Pond, Tropocyclops is subject to predation by notonectids, probably especially B. macrotibialis. Buenoa is common in the open water during the day and probably is more zooplanktivorous than larger notonectids, such as Notonecta, which likely prefer insect prey, at least as later instars (Streams, 1974, 1992; Giller, 1986). Buenoa macrotibialis does in fact readily eat Tropocyclops copepodites and adults (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished) and can dramatically suppress Tropocyclops populations in field enclosures (Hampton et al., 2000). In addition, like zooplanktivorous fish, B. macrotibialis uses vision to feed on Tropocyclops, eating it in the light but not in the dark (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). The typical diel migration of Tropocyclops in Johnson Pond may be an avoidance response to Buenoa. Migrating away from the surface during the day should decrease visual detection by surface-dwelling notonectids. There is, in fact, some evidence that crustacean zooplankton may avoid the surface during the day to escape predation by notonectids. Herwig & Schindler (1996) reported that the experimental removal of Notonecta and other surface-dwelling insects from a fishless pond caused Daphnia to move higher in the water column during the day. Nesbitt, ![Bar graph showing daytime (noon) vertical distributions of P. remata and T. extensus (all stages) averaged over two dates, with percent maximum abundance on the y-axis and depth (m) on the x-axis.](page_1012_1342_484_484.png) Fig. 4 Daytime (noon) vertical distributions of P. remata and T. extensus (all stages) averaged over two dates (see Fig. 3) and expressed as percent maximum abundance. Riessen & Ramcharan (1996) found that the addition of Notonecta to enclosures with Chaoborus induced Daphnia to move lower in the water column during the day. Finally, Dodson (1988) demonstrated in the laboratory that a Notonecta kairomone induced sinking in large species of Daphnia. The diurnal descent of Tropocyclops in Johnson Pond cannot be an avoidance response to Chaoborus. Tropocyclops is eaten by C. flavicans (M.C. Diéguez, unpublished) and probably C. americanus, but these predators remain at or near the bottom during the day and enter the water column only at night (M.C. Dieguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). Thus, during daylight hours Tropocyclops is most abundant nearest the bottom and Chaoborus. The uniform distribution of Tropocyclops across depths at night (Fig. 3) may be because of the fact that temperature, food availability and predation risk at that time were similar across depths. Water temperatures at night varied only from 21 to 22 °C (Fig. 1). Oxygen concentrations at night did decrease with depth but probably were not sufficiently low at 1.0 m (6 ppm, Fig. 1) to be restrictive. Also, potential algal food for Tropocyclops, as estimated from the biovolume of cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates, was quite uniform across depths, especially at night (Fig. 2). Thus, the strategy of many crustacean zooplankton exhibiting typical diel vertical migrations to move up in the water column at night where food is more abundant and temperatures are higher should not apply to Tropocyclops in Johnson Pond. Regarding nocturnal predation, the risk near the surface from Buenoa and Notonecta should be very low. Buenoa is unable to feed effectively on this copepod in the dark or even in full moonlight (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished), and the larger-sized Notonecta should be less able to feed on small zooplankton like Tropocyclops than Buenoa. Chaoborus americanus and C. flavicans certainly prey on Tropocyclops when they are in the water column at night (M.C. Diéguez, unpublished), but their abundance may be similar across depths. Even if these predators were more abundant near the bottom, Tropocyclops may be unable to orient away from them at night. The reverse diel migration of P. remata in Johnson Pond may be an avoidance response to Tropocyclops. During the day when Tropocyclops is most abundant near the bottom, Polyarthra avoids the bottom and is most abundant near the surface (Figs 3 & 4). While T. extensus has been reported to be primarily herbivorous and to have very low feeding rates on small rotifers such as Polyarthra (DeMott & Watson, 1991; Adrian & Frost, 1992), it strongly suppresses P. remata in Johnson Pond. Enclosure experiments showed that population sizes of Polyarthra greatly increased when instar IV Buenoa was present and reduced abundances of Tropocyclops (Hampton et al., 2000). Furthermore, P. remata populations cultured in the laboratory on cryptomonad food grow rapidly in the absence of Tropocyclops but are dramatically suppressed in the presence of Tropocyclops (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). The mechanism by which Tropocyclops inhibits P. remata appears to be direct and to be primarily predation (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). While Polyarthra has an impressive escape response, in which it tumbles many body lengths at about one hundred times its normal swimming speed (Gilbert, 1985), it can be very susceptible to copepod predation (see below). In addition, Tropocyclops could mechanically interfere with Polyarthra. When encountering Polyarthra it could induce escape responses and thereby lead to a considerable expenditure of energy and reduction in feeding time. The diurnal ascent of P. remata is unlikely to be an avoidance response to Chaoborus. While all larval instars of Chaoborus probably readily eat rotifers (Moore & Gilbert, 1987; Moore, 1988; Swift, 1992; Lüning-Krizean, 1997; Wissel & Benndorf, 1998), the later ones select larger, crustacean prey (Moore, 1988; Swift, 1992; Lüning-Krizean, 1997). Polyarthra was consumed by C. punctipennis (Moore & Gilbert, 1987; Moore, 1988), but apparently not at all by C. flavicans (Lüning-Krizean 1997). At any rate, as the Chaoborus in Johnson Pond occur only at or near the bottom sediments during daytime, P. remata would not have to move very far up the water column to avoid this predator. The occurrence of P. remata at the surface of Johnson Pond during the day could make it susceptible to predation by Buenoa. However, even the smallest instars of Buenoa (I and II) cannot eat this rotifer (M.C. Diéguez, unpublished), probably because it is too small (<120 μm) to be visually detected or captured. Early instars of Anisops wakefieldi only ate rotifers larger than 150 μm (Gilbert & Burns, 1999). Therefore, concentration of P. remata at the surface during the day does not put this rotifer at risk from predation by Buenoa. Polyarthra remata in Johnson Pond, just like Tropocyclops, was uniformly distributed across depths at night (Fig. 3). Again, as with Tropocyclops, this probably reflects the fact that there was little variation across depths in temperature, food availability and predation risk. Polyarthra feeds primarily on flagellated cells (Pourriot, 1965; Bogdan & Gilbert, 1984, 1987); therefore, the estimate of similar food availability across depths at night, based on cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates (Fig. 2), probably applies to P. remata as well as to Tropocyclops. As Tropocyclops may be the primary predator of P. remata and is uniformly distributed across depths at night, predation risk to P. remata at night should be similar across depths. Thus, at night P. remata has no spatial refuge from Tropocyclops. It is noteworthy that P. remata was the only rotifer in Johnson Pond to exhibit a diel vertical migration. All other species either were similarly abundant across depths both mid-day and midnight (H. mira, K. cochlearis, A. fissa, As. ovalis) or else were found primarily near the bottom at both times of day (Pl. patulus). Perhaps P. remata is the only rotifer to migrate because it is the most susceptible to predation by Tropocyclops. Despite its escape response, Polyarthra generally is readily eaten, and often selected, by calanoid and cyclopoid copepods (Brandl & Fernando, 1978; Gilbert & Williamson, 1978; Karabin, 1978; Williamson & Gilbert, 1980; Williamson, 1984; Stemberger, 1985; Nero & Sprules, 1986; Williamson & Butler, 1986; Roche, 1990a,b; Adrian, 1991; Paul & Schindler, 1994; Couch, Gilbert & Burns, 1999). This probably is because of its soft body wall and the often limited effectiveness of its escape response against copepod predators. Reasons why the other rotifer species in Johnson Pond might be less susceptible than P. remata to Tropocyclops are not entirely clear. Hexarthra mira also has a soft body wall, but it is almost certainly too large (c. 200 μm) for Tropocyclops to eat. In addition, Hexarthra, like Polyarthra, has an escape response. This response is effective against the predatory rotifer Asplanchna (Sarma, 1993; Iyer & Rao, 1996; Hampton & Starkweather, 1998), and may also be against copepods. Keratella cochlearis is about the same size as P. remata (c. 130 μm, with spines, and 110 μm, respectively), but it has a tough, rigid lorica with anterior and posterior spines which may make it difficult for Tropocyclops to ingest. Several investigators have shown that other copepods have lower feeding rates on K. cochlearis than similarly sized rotifers with softer body walls (Gilbert & Williamson, 1978; Karabin, 1978; Williamson & Butler, 1986; Williamson, 1987; Roche, 1990a,b). Anuraeopsis fissa definitely is small enough (c. 80 μm) to be eaten by Tropocyclops, but it also may have a lorica rigid enough to deter ingestion. However, this species was one of several small rotifers eaten by Boeckella triarticulata and B. hamata (Couch et al., 1999). There appears to be no information on the ability of copepods to prey on Ascomorpha ovalis. This rotifer was very uncommon – mean abundances varied between 2 and 8 individuals L⁻¹ (Fig. 3) – and may have been avoided for this reason. Alternatively, it may be unpalatable. Its congener A. ecaudis is avoided by Diacyclops thomasi, possibly because the mucus house it produces is repellent (Stemberger, 1985, 1987). Mucus production appears to require light (Stemberger, 1987), and hence may depend on the symbiotic algal cells or plastids present in the wall of its stomach (de Beauchamp, 1932, 1965). Ascomorpha ovalis does not produce a mucus house, but it does similarly harbor symbiotic algal cells and possibly plastids (de Beauchamp, 1932, 1965); thus, it may also produce a distasteful mucus. Plationus patulus is a benthic species associated with sediment and aquatic vegetation (Koste, 1978; Koste & Shiel, 1987), and in the laboratory it usually attaches to substrata via a mucus thread (Hampton & Gilbert, 2001). Therefore, its greater abundance near the bottom in Johnson Pond at both mid-day and midnight, and its failure to exhibit a diel migration, was expected. While P. patulus consequently coexists with Tropocyclops near the bottom of the water column during the day, it probably is well defended against it by its size (c. 200 μm) and rigid lorica. There have been many reports of diel vertical migrations in rotifers (Ruttner, 1905; Pennak, 1944; Dumont, 1972; Fairchild et al., 1977; Miracle, 1977; Pivoda, 1977; Cruz-Pizarro, 1978; Magnien & Gilbert, 1983; Carillo, Cruz-Pizarro & Morales-Baquero, 1989; Williamson, 1993; González, 1998; Gilbert & Burns, 2001). However, clear reverse migrations, such as the one displayed by P. remata in Johnson Pond, have been documented only by Dumont (1972), Williamson (1993) and González (1998). In these three cases, the ecological significance of the migration also appears to be avoidance of predation by, or interference from, crustaceans exhibiting typical migrations. In the Dumont study, Asplanchna priodonta migrated out-of-phase with Bosmina spp. and Cyclops vicinus. In the Williamson study, As. ovalis, K. cochlearis and P. vulgaris reduced spatial overlap with Mesocyclops edax. In González’s study, a diurnal ascent of Polyarthra sp. occurred in enclosures without but not with Chaoborus, perhaps to rise above the more dense population of Daphnia pulicaria in the former. In conclusion, the present study in Johnson Pond demonstrates that a zooplankton community may exhibit pronounced vertical differentiation even in a very shallow (1.5 m) water column with little vertical stratification in temperature, dissolved oxygen concentration or phytoplankton. The pronounced diurnal segregation of T. extensus and P. remata may reflect a cascade of strong interspecific behavioural interactions dependent upon the presence of the notonectid Buenoa. In this hypothesized scheme, Tropocyclops migrates towards the bottom to avoid predation by Buenoa near the surface, while Polyarthra, in turn, migrates to the surface to avoid Tropocyclops. The stimuli for these migrations may be kairomones from Buenoa and Tropocyclops, respectively, and are currently under investigation. The migrations should greatly reduce the intensity of interactions between Buenoa and Tropocyclops, and between Tropocyclops and Polyarthra, and therefore promote the coexistence of Tropocyclops and Polyarthra with Buenoa in the ecosystem. In the Dumont study, Asplanchna priodonta migrated out-of-phase with Bosmina spp. and Cyclops vicinus. In the Williamson study, As. ovalis, K. cochlearis and P. vulgaris reduced spatial overlap with Mesocyclops edax. In González’s study, a diurnal ascent of Polyarthra sp. occurred in enclosures without but not with Chaoborus, perhaps to rise above the more dense population of Daphnia pulicaria in the former.

In conclusion, the present study in Johnson Pond demonstrates that a zooplankton community may exhibit pronounced vertical differentiation even in a very shallow (1.5 m) water column with little vertical stratification in temperature, dissolved oxygen concentration or phytoplankton. The pronounced diurnal segregation of T. extensus and P. remata may reflect a cascade of strong interspecific behavioural interactions dependent upon the presence of the notonectid Buenoa. In this hypothesized scheme, Tropocyclops migrates towards the bottom to avoid predation by Buenoa near the surface, while Polyarthra, in turn, migrates to the surface to avoid Tropocyclops. The stimuli for these migrations may be kairomones from Buenoa and Tropocyclops, respectively, and are currently under investigation. The migrations should greatly reduce the intensity of interactions between Buenoa and Tropocyclops, and between Tropocyclops and Polyarthra, and therefore promote the coexistence of Tropocyclops and Polyarthra with Buenoa in the ecosystem.

Differences in the substrate spectrum of extracellular enzymes in shallow lakes of differing trophic status Kai Ziervogel · Dina Leech · Carol Arnosti Received: 29 October 2012 / Accepted: 23 May 2013 / Published online: 6 June 2013 © Springer Science+Business Media Dordrecht 2013 Abstract Organic matter fluxes and food web interactions in lakes depend on the abilities of heterotrophic microbial communities to access and degrade organic matter, a process that begins with extracellular hydrolysis of high molecular weight substrates. In order to determine whether patterns of enzymatic hydrolysis vary among shallow lakes of different trophic status, we investigated the hydrolysis of six specific organic macromolecules (polysaccharides) in the spring and late summer in four adjacent shallow lakes of eutrophic, oligotrophic, and dystrophic status in coastal North Carolina, USA. The spectrum of enzyme activities detected differed strongly between lakes, with all six polysaccharides hydrolyzed in West Mattamuskeet in May, while only two substrates were hydrolyzed in Lake Phelps in August/September. Differences in the spectrum of enzyme activities, and therefore the capabilities of heterotrophic microbial communities, were likely driven by variations among lakes in primary productivity patterns, sediment–water interactions, and/or water chemistry. Our data represent a first step towards a better understanding of carbon substrate availability and differences in carbon cycling pathways in shallow lakes of different trophic status. Keywords Enzymatic activities · Polysaccharide hydrolysis · Carbon cycling · Shallow lakes Introduction Shallow lakes and ponds with an average water depth of less than 3 m are important as habitats and water sources for a wide range of organisms (Scheffer 1998). The state of a lake’s ecosystem and thus the quality of the services provided is determined by the quality of the lake water. Water quality is usually a product of autochthonous and allochthonous carbon inputs, as well as the subsequent cycling of nutrients and carbon through the lake’s food webs (Hamilton and Schladow 1997), a process that is driven primarily by heterotrophic microbial communities (Wetzel 1995; Wetzel and Søndergaard 1997). Rates of organic matter degradation by microbial communities are often determined by the activities of extracellular enzymes, the primary means for microbes to access and degrade organic macromolecules (Chróst 1992; Arnosti 2011). Numerous studies have investigated enzymatic capabilities of microbial communities in a variety of (mainly) deep water lakes (Burns and Dick 2002; Chróst 1991, and references therein), demonstrating a close coupling between enzyme activities and primary productivity (e.g. Chróst and Siuda 2006; Kisand and Tammert 2000). However, microbial dynamics and organic matter fluxes in shallow lakes are likely to be fundamentally different from those of their deep water counterparts because of intense sediment–water interactions and the potentially significant impact of aquatic vegetation. Previous studies of hydrolytic capabilities in lakes—whether deep or shallow—have been conducted using small substrate proxies, consisting of a monomer linked to a fluorophore (Hoppe 1983). The complex constituents of natural organic matter, however, are hydrolyzed by enzymes that are selective for specific aspects of macromolecular structure (e.g. Boraston et al. 2004); small substrate proxies do not adequately represent this structural complexity (Warren 1996). Investigations to date using small substrate proxies therefore provide little information about the abilities of heterotrophic microbial communities to access the range of high molecular weight substrates potentially available for microbial processing in lakes. As a first step in investigating the extent to which pelagic microbial communities in shallow lakes are capable of enzymatically accessing macromolecular substrates, we compared the spectrum of extracellular enzymes hydrolyzing a suite of six specific polysaccharides (pullulan, laminarin, xylan, fucoidan, arabinogalactan, and chondroitin sulfate) in adjacent shallow lakes of different trophic status in North Carolina, USA. Previous work using these polysaccharide substrates in marine, riverine, and estuarine systems has demonstrated that pelagic microbial communities can differ strikingly in their abilities to hydrolyze structurally-related substrates, including those built of the same monomeric constituents (Keith and Arnosti 2001; Steen et al. 2008; Ziervogel and Arnosti 2009; Arnosti et al. 2011). The present study was intended to determine whether different patterns of substrate specificities are also found in shallow lakes of different trophic status. The focus on polysaccharides stems from the fact that they are major constituents of terrestrial as well as aquatic biomass; high molecular weight carbohydrates also make up a significant component of dissolved organic carbon in lakes (Münster 1993). The suite of substrates used in this study includes polysaccharides that are constituents of macroalgae and higher plants (Painter 1983). For example, laminarin, xylan, and fucoidan are found in phytoplankton and algae, while xylan and arabinogalactan are constituents of hemi-celluloses (Painter 1983), which are among the most abundant biopolymers on earth. Pullulan is produced by sea grass epiphytes, and pullulanase functions as a debranching enzyme of starch (White and Kennedy 1988), a common storage polysaccharide of algae (Lee 1980). Chondroitin sulfate is a sulfated glycosaminoglycan produced by mollusks, invertebrates and fish. Laminarin and pullulan are also both soluble glucose-containing polysaccharides, and glucose is one of the most abundant components of total carbohydrates in the environment (Cowie and Hedges 1984; Kennedy and White 1988). Measurements of glucose uptake also demonstrate that this monomer is a major carbon source for bacterioplankton in lakes (Münster 1993, and references therein). This suite of substrates can therefore be used to investigate the ability of heterotrophic microbial communities to initiate the cycling of organic matter that is characteristic of the types that might be found in shallow lakes. Materials and methods Study sites This study was conducted in Lake Mattamuskeet, Pungo Lake, and Lake Phelps, a group of coastal plain shallow lakes in North Carolina, USA, near the Albemarle-Pamlico Sound (Fig. 1; Table 1). Lake Mattamuskeet is a eutrophic–hypereutrophic lake that has been divided into two basins since the construction of a roadway in 1940. Since the lake’s division, macrophytes (mainly water celery or tapegrass) have been the dominant primary producers in the eastern basin (Sponberg and Lodge 2005), resulting in clear water conditions during peak growth in the summer months. The western basin of the lake remains phytoplankton-dominated and thus more turbid throughout the year (note that hereafter the two basins will be treated as two different lakes, i.e. East and West Mattamuskeet; Fig. 1; Table 1). Estimated annual primary productivity of phytoplankton in West Mattamuskeet is 300 g C m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\) compared to <100 g C m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\) of macrophytes; for East Mattamuskeet, annual primary productivity by phytoplankton and macrophytes are 29 and 600 g C m\(^{-2}\) y\(^{-1}\), respectively (phytoplankton data are from M. Piehler Fig. 1 Map of the investigated lakes (1 West Mattamuskeet, 2 East Mattamuskeet, 3 Pungo Lake, 4 Lake Phelps), with pictures of lakes’ water indicating their profound differences in trophic state. Inset for Pungo Lake shows a secchi disk partially submerged in the water (unpublished) and macrophyte data are from Sponberg and Lodge 2005). Pungo Lake is a dystrophic lake loaded with allochthonous carbon throughout the water column, which rapidly attenuates light and thus limits primary productivity (see Fig. 1). Lake Phelps is an oligotrophic clear water lake with sandy sediments throughout the lakebed. Given their close proximity (Fig. 1), the lakes have the same geologic underpinning, experiencing similar wind and precipitation patterns, but their trophic states differ remarkably (Table 1). They have remained internally stable over the last decades, despite similar extent of human impacts through canal construction, decreased forested catchment area, water level maintenance, and agriculture (Waters 2007; Waters et al. 2010). Our current knowledge of the lakes’ ecology and ecosystem responses to nutrient loading and anthropogenic stressors derives from a few recent studies on the paleolimnological sediment records (Waters 2007; Waters et al. 2010). We lack current information of the water quality and ecology of the four lakes, and there are no published data on the lakes’ microbial biomass and community structure. Water sampling The four lakes studied here are part of a national wildlife refuge. For the present study we were able to obtain water samples in May and August/September 2008 (Table 1). Surface water samples were collected by boat from the middle of the lakes, except for East Mattamuskeet in August/September when the water level was too low and the sample was taken near the shore. Prior to water sampling, physico-chemical water parameters were measured using a YSI sensor (Table 1). Water samples were taken from the surface using 250-mL PE bottles (for enzyme activities) and 100-mL dark bottles (for chlorophyll measurements). Samples were stored on ice in a cooler and transported to the laboratory at the UNC Institute of Marine Sciences (Moorhead City, NC) for chlorophyll measurements, and the UNC Department of Marine Sciences (Chapel Hill, NC) for enzyme activity measurements. Chlorophyll was measured in duplicates by filtering 50 mL of lake water GF/F filters that were then placed in 15 mL of 90 % acetone overnight at −20 °C (Holm-Hansen et al. 1965). Samples were run on a Shimadzu Trilogy fluorometer fitted with the non-acidification chlorophyll module. Enzyme activity measurements were initiated 7 days (May) and 9 days (August/September) after collection of water samples following the procedure described below. Enzymatic hydrolysis The six polysaccharide substrates used to measure the spectrum of enzymatic activities were arabinogalactan (mixed polymer of galactose and arabinose), chondroitin sulfate (sulfated polymer of N-acetylgalactosamine and glucuronic acid), fucoidan (sulfated fucose Table 1 Physico-chemical parameters in lake waters at the time of sampling

EM East Mattamuskeet, WM West Mattamuskeet polysaccharide), laminarin (β(1,3)-linked glucose), pullulan (α(1,6)-linked maltotriose (α(1,4)-linked glucose), and xylan (β(1,4)-linked xylose). Unlabeled substrates were obtained from Fluka and Sigma, and fluorescently labeled with fluoresceinamine (FLA) using a modification of the method of Glabe et al. (1983), as described in Arnosti (1996, 2003). Single FLA-polysaccharide substrates were added to 50-ml portions of either unfiltered or autoclaved lake water (the latter served as a killed control) and separated into three clean glass vials, each at 10.5 μM monomer equivalents. Live and control water samples were incubated in the dark at 23 °C (room temperature) for 6 days. One mL per incubation vial was withdrawn immediately after the addition of the substrate, and after 2 as well as 6 days. Samples were filtered through a 0.2-μm pore size syringe filter and stored frozen until analysis. To determine enzymatic hydrolysis rates, samples from each time point were thawed and injected onto a HPLC/gel permeation chromatography (GPC) system consisting of a G-50 Sephadex gel column (20.5 × 1 cm) connected to a G-75 Sephadex gel column (18 × 1 cm). Column outflow passes through a fluorescence detector set to excitation and emission maxima of 490 and 530 nm, respectively. The column set was calibrated with a series of FITC-dextran standards (150, 10, 4 kD, FITC-galactose, and free fluorescent tag). Enzyme activity is measured as the changes in molecular weight of the total added polysaccharide pool over time, hence the requirement for extended incubation times. The information derived from these measurements therefore reflects the potential of heterotrophic microbial communities to access specific substrates, given sufficient time. Such responses potentially include microbial growth, as well as enzyme induction. Substrates incubated with autoclaved lake water showed no significant changes in molecular weights over time. The rates reported here should be regarded as potential hydrolysis rates, since added substrate is in competition with naturally-occurring substrates for enzyme active sites. Given that the level of carbon addition to each incubation (10.5 μM monomer, or 52.5–73.5 μM C) was very similar to previously reported concentrations of total dissolved carbohydrates in lakes (40 nM–60 μM C; Münster1993), hydrolysis rates are most likely zero-order with respect to substrate, and represent maximum potential rates. Statistical analysis Enzyme activities are given as their statistical mean (\( n = 3 \)) ± SD for analytical replicates. Differences of maximum hydrolysis rates measured for each of the six substrates were tested using a two-way ANOVA with lake and sampling time as factors (R Development Core Team 2010). A posthoc comparison using Tukey HSD was applied for significant (\( p \)-values < 0.05) lake-specific differences. Variations in substrate-specific maximum hydrolysis rates between the two sampling times were determined for each lake individually using a \( t \) test (Excel® data analysis toolpack). Results Physico-chemical parameters of the four lakes were very different between the two sampling times (Table 1). Surface water temperatures in the four lakes in August/September were 26–30 °C and thus 6 °C (Lake Phelps) to 10 °C (Pungo Lake) warmer compared to May; oxygen saturation levels were accordingly lower at higher water temperatures. Chlorophyll concentrations at both sampling times were generally highest in the eutrophic East and West Mattamuskeet and lowest in the oligotrophic Lake Phelps. Water conductivity in both basins of Lake Mattamuskeet was higher in August/September compared to May, and remained at the same level in the other two lakes. We also found considerably lower pH in August/September compared to May in three (East Mattamuskeet, Phelps, Pungo) of the four lakes. The difference in pH between the two sampling times was most pronounced in Pungo Lake, where pH dropped from 8.8 in May to 5.4 in August/September. Lake Phelps’ and East Mattamuskeets’ pH decreased from 6.2 and 8.6 in May to 4.9 and 7.6 in August/September, respectively. Along with changes in water chemistry and temperature, the four lakes showed distinct lake-specific as well as sampling time-specific differences in the spectrum of enzymatic activities (note that all polysaccharide incubations were conducted at constant room temperature, not in situ temperature, so temperature effects were not explicitly considered). The broadest enzymatic spectrum was measured in West Mattamuskeet, where all six substrates were hydrolyzed in May and all except fucoidan were hydrolyzed in August/September (Fig. 2a; Table 2). In East Mattamuskeet, in contrast, only 4 substrates (arabinogalactan, chondroitin, laminarin, xylan) were hydrolyzed at both sampling times (Fig. 2b; Table 2). An even narrower spectrum of polysaccharide hydrolases was measured in Lake Phelps and Pungo Lake: three (chondroitin, laminarin, xylan) and two substrates (laminarin, xylan) were hydrolyzed in Lake Phelps in May and August/September, respectively (Fig. 2c; Table 2), and only laminarin and xylan were hydrolyzed in Pungo Lake during both sampling times (Fig. 2d; Table 2). Maximum hydrolysis rate measured for each substrate varied significantly between lakes and sampling time (ANOVA; Table 3). Generally highest hydrolysis rates were found in the two basins of Lake Mattamuskeet, except for xylan, which was hydrolyzed at highest rates in Pungo Lake in May (Tables 2, 3). Considering each lake separately, we also found differences in hydrolysis rates for five of the six substrates between the two sampling times (t test; Table 3). Higher hydrolysis rates in May compared to August/September were found for xylan in West Mattamuskeet, Lake Phelps, and Pungo Lake, for chondroitin in West Mattamuskeet. Hydrolysis rates in August/September were higher for xylan and arabinogalactan in East Mattmuskeet, and for pullulan in West Mattmuskeet. Only lake-specific laminarin hydrolysis rates in May and August/September were statistically indistinguishable from one another. Differences in primary productivity (and potentially in hydrology) between these likes likely drive the remarkable differences in enzymatic capabilities of their respective microbial communities, as shown by the differences in the spectrum of substrates hydrolyzed (Tables 2, 3). All six substrates were only hydrolyzed in West Mattamuskeet in May when three (chondroitin, fucoidan, xylan) of the six substrates also showed higher maximum hydrolysis rates compared to August/September (Table 3). Neither fucoidan nor pullulan were hydrolyzed in East Mattamuskeet; in Lake Phelps and Pungo Lake, pullulan, fucoidan, and arabinogalactan were not hydrolyzed (Fig. 2; Table 2). The broad enzymatic spectrum observed in West Mattamuskeet reflects the ability of the bacterial community to degrade a diverse DOM pool that was likely dominated by phytoplankton primary productivity at the time of sampling. Phytoplankton are the dominant primary producers in the western basin of Lake Mattamuskeet, where overall highest oxygen saturation levels in the water column were measured in May (Table 1), suggesting elevated photosynthetic activities and thus phytoplankton metabolism at the first sampling time. Phytoplankton-derived DOM can include a wide range of carbohydrates, which may explain the broader range of substrates hydrolyzed in May relative to August/September. Phytoplankton exopolymeric substances, for example, have been found to be enriched in deoxysugar-containing sulfated polysaccharides, a description that fits fucoidan (Mopper et al. 1995). The narrower spectrum of polysaccharide hydrolases in East Mattamuskeet suggests a less diverse carbohydrate pool, or less diverse capabilities of the microbial communities to access substrates compared to West Mattamuskeet. We sampled at the beginning and at the end of the macrophyte growing season in East Mattamuskeet, assuming that macrophyte-DOM was a major carbohydrate source in the eastern basin at both sampling times. Bacterial decomposition of high levels of macrophyte DOM at the end of the growing season in East Mattamuskeet may explain significantly higher xylanase and arabinogalactan hydrolase activity in August/September compared to May (Tables 2, 3). Xylan hydrolysis in August/September was more than double the rate measured in May, and constituted more than half of the summed enzyme activities (Fig. 2; Table 2). Lake Phelps and Pungo Lake showed lower hydrolysis rates and lower functional diversity with respect to polysaccharide hydrolysis compared to East and West Mattamuskeet (Table 3). This difference may be a result of markedly lower primary productivity of the oligotrophic Lake Phelps, and the dystrophic waters of Pungo Lake (Table 1). In this context, the lack of hydrolysis of arabinogalactan in Lake Phelps and Pungo Lake is notable, since arabinogalactans are common constituents of hemicelluloses (Painter 1983), and are thus widespread in terrestrial ecosystems. Despite the obvious presence of humic substances in Pungo Lake (presumably due to allochthonous input into the lake, necessarily derived from terrestrial production), no arabinogalactan hydrolysis was observed in either this lake or in the clear water Lake Phelps. For shallow lakes such as these, the extent of sediment resuspension (which is far greater than in deep water lakes; Scheffer 1998) may also provide an explanation for the differences in the spectrum of substrates hydrolyzed in West and East Mattamuskeet. East Mattamuskeet is likely less prone to sediment resuspension events compared to West Mattamuskeet, which lacks the lake bed-stabilizing macrophytes. In general, mixing between the sediment and the overlying water can enhance the vertical transport of sediment-associated benthic microorganisms (e.g. Ritzrau and Graf 1992), increasing rates of enzyme activities in waters affected by sediment resuspension (Chróst and Riemann 1994; Cotner 2000; Ritzrau and Graf 1992; Ritzrau 1996; Wainright 1990). In addition to enhanced hydrolysis rates, sediment resuspension has been found to widen the spectrum of water column enzyme activities in coastal marine systems. Using the same suite of six polysaccharide substrates, Ziervogel and Arnosti (2009) found that sediment resuspension widened the spectrum from four to all six polysaccharide hydrolases in estuarine waters, likely reflecting a wider range of enzymatic capabilities of marine benthic microorganisms relative to bacterioplankton (Arnosti 2000, 2008; Teske et al. 2011; Ziervogel and Arnosti 2008). Comparisons of the spectrum of high molecular weight substrates hydrolyzed in benthic and pelagic lacustrine environments remain to be carried out. Published comparisons of enzyme activities in pelagic and benthic lacustrine environments are limited to a single study demonstrating more rapid hydrolysis of a wide range of small substrate proxies in sediments compared to overlying lake waters (Chróst and Siuda 2002). Differences in enzymatic capabilities of the microbial communities of these four lakes may also reflect the functional outcome of fundamental differences in the community structure of oligotrophic, dystrophic, and eutrophic lakes. Bacterial community structure in shallow lakes has been found to correlate with the lakes’ trophic status and suspended matter load (van der Gucht et al. 2005; Muylaert et al. 2002). Water chemistry can also lead to changes in the diversity of bacterial communities of a lake (Methe and Zehr 1999; Percent et al. 2008). Pungo Lake and Lake Phelps experienced a much larger drop in pH between May and August/September (Table 1) than did East Mattamuskeet; we hypothesize that this change in pH may have affected the lakes’ microbial communities. A reduction in community diversity in lower pH waters has been demonstrated by compositional analysis of the bacterial communities in 18 lakes affected by various degrees of acidic deposition (Percent et al. 2008). Reduced community diversity, caused by significant changes in water column pH between May and August/September, may also lead to a reduction in functional capabilities among the community members robust enough to withstand rapidly changing pH. Our initial investigation of geographically-proximate lakes of different trophic status demonstrates that the enzymatic capabilities of lacustrine pelagic communities differ profoundly from one another. Comparable differences in the spectrum of enzyme activities in marine pelagic systems have been found only across much broader spatial gradients (Arnosti et al. 2011). Determining the fundamental factors underlying these differences in enzymatic capabilities will require a coordinated study that integrates microbial community composition and metabolism with detailed analysis of organic matter sources and composition. Given that shallow lakes dominate the areal extent of inland waters (Downing 2010), which play an important role in global carbon cycling (Tranvik et al. 2009), better understanding of the breadth of substrates potentially available to microbial communities in shallow lakes will improve our abilities to understand disparate means of carbon cycling in these lakes, and ultimately to predict and model carbon transformations and CO₂ fluxes between inland waters and the atmosphere. Factors influencing macroinvertebrate assemblages in artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan Sen-Her Shieh · Yao-Sheng Chi Received: 21 August 2009/Revised: 14 April 2010/Accepted: 17 April 2010/Published online: 2 May 2010 © Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2010 Abstract Macroinvertebrate assemblages and its association with environmental factors at the 11 artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan were examined using the multivariate analysis software STATICO. The aims of the study were to determine whether spatial and seasonal variation of macroinvertebrate assemblages changed seasonally, to examine which environmental factors determined the spatial and temporal structure of maroinvertebrate assemblages, and to compare between-pond variations in the taxon composition of macroinvertebrates. Macroinvertebrates were collected seasonally by a corer and a sweep net in 2007, and 13 physical and chemical factors were measured at the same time. A total of 31 macroinvertebrate taxa were collected during the sampling period, and the most dominant taxa were Chironomidae (31.7% of total animal abundance) and Tubificidae (22.4%). STATICO identified pond size, pond depth, sediment depth, and altitude as the major abiotic factors and Bufo melanostictus (Amphibia) as the major biotic factor to influence macroinvertebrate assemblages at these ponds. These factors changed with seasonality. For example, the abundance of B. melanostictus was the most important factor during the spring but became much less important in other seasons. According to the spatial distribution patterns of macroinvertebrate assemblages, macroinvertebrates could be split into two groups based on their dispersal. The active dispersers, such as insect taxa, were strongly associated with pond size and the passive dispersers, such as non-insect taxa, were strongly associated with the pond depth and/or sediment depth. The results of this study suggested that pond size might influence macroinvertebrate assemblages through their dispersal mechanisms and that the environmental factors which influenced the macroinvertebrate assemblages most changed with seasons in this study area. Keywords Pond size · Active dispersers · Passive dispersers · STATICO Introduction Ponds are rich and diverse habitats and play a key role in safeguarding aquatic biodiversity. They are defined as waterbodies between 1 m^2 and 2 ha in area which may be permanent or seasonal, including both artificial and natural waterbodies (Biggs et al., 2005). Despite their small surface area, they are exceptionally rich in biodiversity, as compared to streams and large lakes, and contribute significantly to regional freshwater biodiversity in many northern temperate regions (Oertli et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2003; Nicolet et al., 2004), but our understanding of the relative biodiversity importance of ponds elsewhere remains limited. However, the ponds are threatened due to anthropogenic activities, such as eutrophication, chemical pollution, acid rain, physical destruction, and invasion of exotic species (Heath & Whitehead, 1992; Brönmark & Hansson, 2002; Boothby, 2003). While monitoring programs for freshwaters have been widely carried out in many countries, particularly for streams and lakes, these programs have largely failed to include ponds (Oertli et al., 2005). The macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds are influenced by both abiotic and biotic factors. Abiotic factors, such as pond size (Rundle et al., 2002) and water chemistry (Friday, 1987), affect the number of taxa in the community. It has been suggested that large ponds support more macroinvertebrate taxa than small ones due to habitat heterogeneity (Della Bella et al., 2005). Biotic factors, such as the presence or absence of large predators (fish and amphibians) in a pond and the dispersal ability of macroinvertebrates, appear to be important in determining macroinvertebrate assemblages. Invertebrate biomass was found to be higher in fishless wetlands than in wetlands with fish (Zimmer et al., 2001). Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that the taxon richness of active dispersal macroinvertebrates was positively correlate with pond size, whereas the taxon richness of passive macroinvertebrates did not correlated with environmental variables. Assessing these influences on macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds are a key process to understand community structure and succession and to propose a man-made control before any pollution resulting from anthropogenic activities could occur. The relationships between environmental factors and macroinvertebrate distributions in freshwaters have often been studied using principal component analysis (Hinden et al., 2005), canonical correspondence analysis (Williams et al., 2003; Nicolet et al., 2004; Carchini et al., 2005), multidimensional scaling (Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006, 2009), or clustering (Collinson et al., 1995; Nicolet et al., 2004; Bilton et al., 2006). The main drawback of these methods is that they do not consider that both environmental factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages vary temporally and that the former affects the latter. In order to overcome this problem, the STATICO (STATIS and CO-inertia) has been developed (Thioulouse et al., 2004). It is a multivariate method allowing simultaneous analysis of a sequence of paired ecological tables recorded through a series of sampling occasions. Thioulouse et al. (2004) pointed that STATICO is particularly suited to study the relationship between the environmental and taxonomic tables when both vary time. Since ponds are not uniform as revealed by their shape, shoreline, and size, and a clear seasonal dynamics has been observed for the difference macroinvertebrate assemblages (Studinski & Grubbs, 2007), STATICO is a well-suited statistical tool to get a clear representation of the spatial and temporal variation of the macroinvertebrates assemblages in ponds. Most studies which examined macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds were conducted in Europe (Oertli et al., 2009). There are still relatively few such studies in Asia, especially artificial ponds, where the biodiversity has been poorly investigated. Because of the complexity of pond systems affected spatially and temporally by various abiotic and biotic factors, we analyzed using STATICO the relationships between these factors and maroinvertebrate assemblages in the 11 artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan. The first aim of the study was to determine whether spatial and seasonal variation of macroinvertebrate assemblages changed among these subtropical ponds where seasonality was insignificant. The second aim was to examine which abiotic and biotic factors determined the spatial and temporal structure of these macroinvertebrate assemblages at these ponds. We assumed that the pond size and the presence and absence of large predators in ponds should be the most important factors to affect macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds. Therefore, it was predicted that ponds which were large and/or without large predators should support more taxon richness than ponds which were small and/or with large predators. The final aim was to compare between-pond variations in the taxon composition of active and passive dispersers of macroinvertebrates. We assumed that the active dispersal macroinvertebrate should be more associated with pond size. Materials and methods Study area Sampling sites were established in the coastal area of west central Taiwan. The area represents one of the biotopes most severely threatened by human impacts since the main land use of the area is municipal and agricultural. The area is flat, has low altitude (<300 m.a.s.l.), and has the annual precipitation of about 1,405 mm between 1998 and 2007, with the perhumid season from April to September and the relative drought season from October to December. Annual mean air temperature is about 23.2°C. The dominant vegetation of the area is Panicum maximum (Poaceae) and Acacia confuse (Fabaceae). Because our aims were to assess the relationships between environmental factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages among different ponds, 11 artificial ponds were selected in this area to insure that they were influenced by the same climate condition and land use. These ponds are situated in school grounds and located between the coordinates 24°6′N, 120°31′E and 24°24′N, 120°38′E. Sampling methods Macroinvertebrates samples were collected in January (winter), April (spring), July (summer), and October (autumn) 2007. Because different habitats and groups of macroinvertebrates require different sampling methods, the use of a single method for all habitats could yield misleading conclusion on macroinvertebrate richness. Therefore, two methods, e.g., the quantitative and qualitative methods (Studinski & Grubbs, 2007) were used in this study. A benthic corer sampler (diameter = 26 cm) was used as a quantitative method. During each sampling occasion, the longest transect of the pond was selected, and three benthic samples were taken at 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of this transect. The benthic corer was pushed into the substrate until it reached an impermeable layer. The sediments within the corer were transferred by a hand with a cup to a bucket. Animals, organic matter, and remaining water in bucket were passed through a sieve with 0.8-mm apertures. These materials were preserved in 95% ethanol in the field. This procedure allowed us to sample benthic macroinvertebrates. For the qualitative method, ponds were sampled with a sweep net (with 20-cm D-frame and 200-μm mesh) at different microhabitats (such as emergent and submerged aquatic vegetation and pond margins) for 5 min (Batzer et al., 2004). This method allowed us to collect nekton macroinvertebrates and to get a representative sample from the system (Collinson et al., 1995). Sample sizes and sampling time were decided after a pilot study undertaken in these ponds. The main outcomes of this pilot study were that three corer samples and a total time of 5 min were good enough to have the representative taxa for these ponds. In the laboratory, all the samples were rinsed by tap water, and the animals were sorted and preserved in 75% ethanol for further analysis. The macroinvertebrate taxa were identified to the lowest taxonomic unit possible. Aquatic insects were identified according to Morse et al. (1994) and other macroinvertebrate taxa according to Dudgeon (1999) and Shy & Yu (1998). Members of Ostracoda were not identified further. Three vertebrate taxa were collected in this study, and they were common Asian toad (Bufo melanostictus), mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis), and paradise fish (Macropodus opercularis). Both B. melanostictus and G. affinis were almost found in each of the sampling ponds and were abundant, and so the two species were included in the following analyses. The physical and chemical factors were measured at each of the 11 ponds on each sampling occasion. Conductivity, pH value, dissolved oxygen, and water temperature were measured using WTW multi 340i. Water depth and sediment depth were measured using a graduated stick at 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of the longest transect. The shoreline and area of ponds were assessed with a measuring tape by pacing in field. The shoreline development index (SDI) was calculated as follows: \[ \text{SDI} = \frac{L}{2 \sqrt{\pi A}} \] where \( L \) = the length of shoreline, and \( A \) = the area of pond (Wetzel, 2001). Finally, the percentage of plant cover at each sampling pond was measured by taking the pictures. The relative area of plant cover was estimated by ImageJ 1.42 software. Data analysis For each sampling occasion, three benthic corer samples were combined together as a sample unit and mean densities, taxon richness, Gastropoda richness, and Odonata richness were calculated as community parameters. Simple correlations between community parameters and environmental factors were made by the Spearman rank correlation test. Since the data sets of environmental variables were not normal and had no constant variance, the Kruskal–Wallis H test was used to test the differences of environmental factors among different ponds (Zar, 1999). Duncan’s multiple range test was conducted at a significance level of \( P < 0.05 \). STATICO was used to assess the spatial variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages and its dynamics in time and examine the dynamic trajectories of the physicochemical factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages. Before STATICO was carried out, data were organized into a succession of coupled environmental and taxonomic tables, each pair of tables corresponding to a sampling period. Four temporal pairs of tables (four sampling dates) were used in this study. Each table was first analyzed by principal component analysis (PCA), and each pair was then linked by a co-inertial analysis (Dray et al., 2003), producing a cross table. Partial triadic analysis (PTA) (Thioulouse & Chessel, 1987) was then used to analyze the series of cross tables. PTA involves three successive steps (Thioulouse et al., 2004). (1) The interstructure analysis gives the importance of each table and summarizes the global structure and the relationship between the tables. (2) The compromise analysis gives a picture of the structures common to all the tables. (3) The trajectory analysis summarizes the variability of the series of tables around the common structure defined by the compromise. In this analysis, three benthic corer and sweep samples for each pond on each sampling date were pooled together. Those taxa, which occurred only on one sampling date and their abundance were less than 1% of total abundance on the sampling date, were excluded from the analysis. A total of 21 taxa were included in the data set. Two vertebrate taxa, B. melanostictus and G. affinis, were used as environmental factors to detect their effect on macroinvertebrate assemblages. The relationships between pond size and shoreline length and between water temperature and dissolved oxygen were highly correlated, and so shoreline length and dissolved oxygen were excluded in this analysis. In total, therefore, 13 environmental factors were used in the analysis. All environmental factors, except pH values, and the macroinvertebrate abundances were \( \log(x + 1) \) transformed to approach a normal distribution (Legendre & Legendre, 1998). The analysis was performed with the ADE-4 software (Thioulouse et al., 1997). Results Environmental factors Environmental factors showed spatial differences among sampling ponds and temporal differences among seasons (Table 1). The mean conductivity of ponds varied from 148 to 783 \( \mu \)s/cm (mean = 288 \( \pm \) 54 (S.E.) \( \mu \)s/cm, median = 243 \( \mu \)s/cm). The high conductivity at site 2 was probably due to the location of pond 2 which was near the coast. Low dissolved oxygen was found at all ponds (mean = 3.13 \( \pm \) 0.37 mg/l, median = 3.23 mg/l). This reflected the fact that these ponds were more or less affected by human activities due to their location. With the exception of pond 10 (pH = 6.84), all ponds possessed pH values above 7.0. All ponds had mean water temperature between 21.6 and 24.7\( ^\circ \)C with the lowest in winter (9.9\( ^\circ \)C at site 1–15.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 6) and the highest in summer (27.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 10–31.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 4). The mean depth of ponds ranged between 15.1 and 42.8 cm (mean = 29.1 \( \pm \) 3.0 cm, median = 30 cm). The sediment depth of ponds varied from 0.8 to 6.2 cm (mean = 2.18 \( \pm \) 0.47 cm, median = 1.6 cm). Macroinvertebrate communities In total, 31 macroinvertebrate taxa were recorded at the 11 sampling ponds during the sampling year (Table 2). In terms of taxon richness, pond fauna were dominated by Gastropoda, of which 10 taxa were recorded. Odonata were represented by nine taxa. Compared with Gastropoda and Odonata, Hemiptera (3 taxa), Hirudinea (2), Ephemeroptera (2), Decopoda (1), Coleoptera (1), Diptera (1), Oligochaeta (1), and Ostracoda (1) were relatively poor. For Diptera, Oligochaeta, and Ostracoda, it is likely to be an underestimate of the species-level diversity in these sampled ponds. The total macroinvertebrate species richness of ponds ranged between 2 and 13 (mean = 7.2 \( \pm \) 1.4 S.E.; median = 6) (Table 2). The abundance of B. melanostictus varied from 0 to 95.6% of total number of animals. The results were associated with the fact that the higher the temperature, the higher the number of gastropod and odonate taxa. In contrast, the number of individuals and taxa were negatively correlated with the altitudes of ponds. Interstructure The interstructure factor maps of the STATICO showed that the decrease of the eigenvalues was high between the first and second eigenvalues (59.3 and 16.3% of the total inertia, respectively) (Fig. 1A). This suggested that only the first axis might be chosen for the compromise analysis. The correlation circle showed all the sampling dates displaying same sign on the first interstructure factor (axis 1), indicating a positive correlation between the corresponding set of matrices (Fig. 1A). Such a uniform distribution on the first axis indicated a strong common structure of seasonality. The structure expressed through the first axis of the interstructure, therefore, corresponded to a community spatial pattern common to the different sampling dates. The second interstructure factor was characterized by the opposition between the sampling dates of winter and spring (positive correlation with axis 2) against the sampling dates of summer and autumn (negatively correlated with the axis). Compromise The contribution of the different sampling dates to the construction of the compromise table was similar (weights from 0.485 to 0.515) (Fig. 1D). Therefore, each of the four samplings played a similar role in the construction of the compromise table. Moreover, the fit of each of the tables to the compromise table (\( \cos^2 \)) was homogeneous (from 0.70 in autumn to 0.80 in winter). Out of the 13 environmental factors taken into account, only a few were found to be correlated with the structure of macroinvertebrate assemblages (Fig. 1B). The first axis described a positive association with the sediment depth, water temperature, and distance from the major water bodies, and a negative association with the altitude. The second axis was mainly positively associated with pond depth but negatively with the pond size. The correspondence with the macroinvertebrate taxa allowed identifying these taxa which responded to the environmental gradients (Fig. 1C). On the first axis, the most abundant taxa (Tubificidae, Planorbidae, Ischnura senegalensis, and Physa acuta) caught in the ponds with deeper sediment and higher water temperature but with lower abundance of B. melanostictus were opposed to the taxa (Neocaridina denticulata) in the ponds with higher altitude. On the second axis, the most abundant taxa (Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) caught in the ponds with larger pond size which was opposed to the taxa (Tubificidae, Austropeplea ollula, and Melanoides tuberculatus tubercul) in the ponds with greater depth, higher plant cover, and higher abundance of Gambusia affinis. In addition, it was found that most insect taxa (e.g., Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) were located at the lower left part of the figure and associated with the pond size. The most non-insect taxa were located at the upper part of the figure and associated with the pond depth, except P. acuta, P. canaliculata, and Planorbidae which were associated with sediment depth. Trajectories The trajectories factor maps indicated that the relationships between the most abundant taxa in the assemblages and environmental factors differed between sampling periods (Figs. 2, 3). The stable part of the macroinvertebrate-environment dynamics was well expressed by the autumn survey due to the closer clustering around the center of the plot. The maps also enabled us to identify seasonal variations of the position of taxa around the common structure. In winter, Tubificidae and Ostracoda were positively associated with the pond depth, sediment depth, water temperature, and distance from the major water bodies but Chironomidae, Notonectidae, Orthetrum sabina, and P. acuta were positively associated with the pond size. In spring, the major macroinvertebrate taxa were I. senegalensis, P. acuta, Tubificidae, and A. ollula, and they were negatively associated with the abundance of B. melanostictus. In summer, I. senegalensis and Chironomidae were positively associated with the pond size, and Tubificidae was positively associated with the pond depth. In autumn, the pond size was the major factor to affect the abundance of Pomacea canaliculata, O. sabina, and I. senegalensis, and the pond depth were the major factors to affect the abundance of A. ollula and Tubificidae. Discussion The composition of macroinvertebrate assemblages The importance of ponds as a habitat of aquatic macroinvertebrates has been emphasized until recently (Biggs et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2009). Bilton et al. (2009) studied ponds in two areas of southern England and found that the means of species richness of macroinvertebrates in each pond were 19.7 and 22.0, indicating the importance of such habitat in biodiversity. While the mean taxon richness in this study is lower than that found by Bilton et al. (2009), this is perhaps not surprising, as these ponds are relatively new, artificial ponds which are impacted by human activity. The result, therefore, might reflect the fact that the ponds sampled are not likely to be representative of less impacted sites in the region. Besides, the result might also reflect the fact that figures represented considerable underestimates of the true taxon richness of these ponds. For instance, the Chironomidae in this study were only simply enumerated. Many studies (Street & Titmus, 1979; Hinden et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006) have pointed to the high diversity of chironomids in small ponds. The studied ponds, therefore, may be important for the freshwater biodiversity in this relatively impacted landscape, but more “natural” ponds elsewhere in the region are likely to hold more species. Moreover, this study found more taxon richness than Fig. 2 Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. See Table 2 for the taxonomic abbreviations ![Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007.](page_320_180_1408_1092.png) the study of Lin et al. (2006) which found 4.6 taxa per pond in eight alpine ponds (>3,000 m.a.s.l.) in central Taiwan, indicating that taxon richness in Taiwan ponds was related to altitude, with increasing altitude being associated with a reduction in species richness. Hinden et al. (2005) also indicated that an altitude-related decline in taxon richness in the ponds of Switzerland. Carchini et al. (2005) pointed out that ponds at high altitude in central Italy had lower odonate richness than those at low altitude. Similarly, in this study, the average number of odonate richness in each pond was 1.8 (S.E. = 0.4), rising to 2.50 (S.E. = 0.38) when the pond without odonate were excluded. This was higher than the average of 0.88 (S.E. = 0.13) taxa per pond found in the high altitude ponds in central Taiwan (Lin et al., 2006). Similarly, while 10 gastropod taxa were found in this study, none was found by Lin et al. (2006). Many studies showed that Chironomidae and Coleoptrea typically made up the majority of the macroinvertebrate species richness in ponds worldwide (Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006, 2009). In our study, we also found that ponds were predominated by chironomids at ponds 1, 2, 3, and 7. However, only one taxon of aquatic beetles was found in any of our ponds under this study. It was probably due to the fact that these ponds were located at urban area and were relatively impacted sites. Therefore, they have much smaller regional species pools. Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that aquatic beetles are amongst vagile aquatic insect taxa. They would not access the ponds if these ponds are less suitable for their colonization. The result of this study might reflect the fact that these ponds, being in an urban area, were relatively impacted, should affect aquatic beetles more than other taxa. In this study, the most abundant taxa were chironomids and tubificids. The result was in accordant with the suggestion of Batzer et al. (2004) that most successful macroinvertebrates in ponds may be habitat generalists. They further suggested that the variation of these taxa among ponds might be largely stochastic. In this Fig. 3 Trajectories factor map of environmental variables using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. See Table 1 for the environmental abbreviations ![Trajectories factor map of environmental variables using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007.](page_370_180_1407_1207.png) study, however, we found that the distributions of the chironomids and tubificids were mostly associated with the pond size and pond depth, respectively. Macroinvertebrate assemblages and environmental factors The results of STATICO suggested that the main common features of the organization patterns were first, the sediment depth and altitude, and second, the pond size and pond depth (Fig. 1B). Water chemistry, such as pH and conductivity values, seemed not to be important environmental factors to affect macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. In contrast, Friday (1987) suggested that water chemistry was an important factor to shape macroinvertebrate assemblages. In addition, we found that the total macroinvertebrate taxa were not correlated with the pond age (Fig. 1B; Table 3). This finding concurred with the results of Jeffries (1991) and Gee et al. (1997) but contrasted with the result of Barnes (1983). Gee et al. (1997) indicated that invertebrate richness might be related to the age of the ponds whereas ponds were isolated from other wetlands. This was not the case in this study, because all the ponds in this study were not far away from the major water bodies (Table 1). Also, these ponds are relatively of recent origin. The strength of an age signal will depend on the relative importance of other drivers structuring the communities. Many studies (Oertli et al., 2002; Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2009) found that the pond size and depth showed strong relationships with species’ occurrence across ponds. STATICO also identified pond size and depth as major environmental factors to influence macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. The influence of pond size and depth on macroinvertebrate assemblages was generally a consequence of greater habitat heterogeneity (Della Bella et al., 2005), lower extinction risk due to larger population sizes (Gee et al., 1997), and buffering against fluctuations in physicochemical conditions in larger ponds (Connor & McCoy, 1979). In our study, however, we found that insect taxa, active dispersers, were highly associated with pond size and most non-insect taxa, passive dispersers, were associated with pond depth and/or sediment depth (Fig. 1B, C). Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that invertebrate taxa with different dispersal mechanisms show different distribution patterns across habitat gradients of size. Active dispersers show significant positive relationships with pond size and lead to non-random patterns in species distribution between ponds. The response of the passive taxa to depth might relate to relative permanence—deeper (and hence more permanent) ponds favoring desiccation-prone taxa such as molluscs. The effects of dispersal mechanisms on distribution patterns might reflect the lack of depth and area effects on taxon richness (Table 3). Similarly, Jeffries (1991) was unable to find a significant area effect on the richness of macroinvertebrates and suggested that other factors, such as biotic interactions, might be important. The biotic interactions, such as the presence or absence of fish or amphibian predators in a pond, appeared to be important in determining the abundance of macroinvertebrates (Zimmer et al., 2001). In this study, we found that ponds without amphibian predators contained more macroinvertebrate taxa than those with amphibian predators when pond 1 was excluded in the analysis. For instance, ponds 5, 10, and 11 which possessed relatively high abundance of B. melanostictus had only 2–4 macroinvertebrate taxa (Table 2). However, there was no evidence to show that fishless ponds (pond 5) contain more invertebrate taxa than those with fish. There might be other factors that explain the low taxon richness at pond 1. Similarly, the ponds described by Gee et al. (1997) as fish ponds were the most taxonomically rich amongst of those they sampled. On the other hand, abundance and species richness of odonate predators, such as I. senegalensis, O. sabina sabina, and P. flavescens, were little associated with the presence of B. melanostictus (Fig. 2B, C). This result was expected for amphibian because the predation of amphibian on odonate was low (Corbet, 1999). Seasonal variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages As we know, most studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds focused on the effects of hydroperiod of temporary ponds on macroinvertebrate assemblages (e.g., Brooks, 2000, Batzer et al., 2004). There were very few studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in permanent ponds. From the results of STATICO, the spatial patterns of macroinvertebrate assemblages at the 11 ponds were highly persistent during the course of the four seasons. Only a very limited number of taxa exhibited a strong variation of their abundance over seasons. The variations mainly reflected the shift in water temperatures which were negatively associated with altitude. Most taxa were positively correlated with water temperature (Fig. 1C). Both abundance and taxon richness of gastropod and odonate was positively related to water temperature (Table 3). Smith et al. (2003) also found similar results for gastropods. The seasonal variation was probably due to life-history patterns related to reproduction, dispersal, predation, temperature, and food (Tangen et al., 2003). The environmental factors which influenced the macroinvertebrate assemblages most in these ponds also changed with seasons. For example, pond size, though positively correlated with the sediment depth gradient in spring, became less correlated during the winter and summer. The abundance of B. melanostictus was inversely correlated with sediment depth and pond depth during the spring, and became the most important environmental factor during the spring, but was not correlated with them at the other seasons. In conclusion, macroinvertebrate assemblages varied spatially and temporally in response to the abiotic and biotic factors of these artificial subtropical ponds. Pond size, pond depth, sediment depth, altitude, and distance from the major water bodies were the major abiotic factors to determine the macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, and the abundances of B. melanostictus were the major biotic factors. However, these factors changed with seasonality. According to the spatial distribution of macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, macroinvertebrates could be classified into two groups based on their dispersal mechanisms. The active dispersers, such as insect taxa, were mostly associated with pond size, and the passive dispersers, such as non-insect taxa, with pond depth and sediment depth. The effect of pond size on macroinvertebrate assemblages might be through the dispersal mechanisms of macroinvertebrates. This effect needs to be further studied in the future. Since the data sets of environmental variables were not normal and had no constant variance, the Kruskal–Wallis H test was used to test the differences of environmental factors among different ponds (Zar, 1999). Duncan’s multiple range test was conducted at a significance level of \( P < 0.05 \).

STATICO was used to assess the spatial variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages and its dynamics in time and examine the dynamic trajectories of the physicochemical factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages. Before STATICO was carried out, data were organized into a succession of coupled environmental and taxonomic tables, each pair of tables corresponding to a sampling period. Four temporal pairs of tables (four sampling dates) were used in this study. Each table was first analyzed by principal component analysis (PCA), and each pair was then linked by a co-inertial analysis (Dray et al., 2003), producing a cross table. Partial triadic analysis (PTA) (Thioulouse & Chessel, 1987) was then used to analyze the series of cross tables. PTA involves three successive steps (Thioulouse et al., 2004). (1) The interstructure analysis gives the importance of each table and summarizes the global structure and the relationship between the tables. (2) The compromise analysis gives a picture of the structures common to all the tables. (3) The trajectory analysis summarizes the variability of the series of tables around the common structure defined by the compromise. In this analysis, three benthic corer and sweep samples for each pond on each sampling date were pooled together. Those taxa, which occurred only on one sampling date and their abundance were less than 1% of total abundance on the sampling date, were excluded from the analysis. A total of 21 taxa were included in the data set. Two vertebrate taxa, B. melanostictus and G. affinis, were used as environmental factors to detect their effect on macroinvertebrate assemblages. The relationships between pond size and shoreline length and between water temperature and dissolved oxygen were highly correlated, and so shoreline length and dissolved oxygen were excluded in this analysis. In total, therefore, 13 environmental factors were used in the analysis. All environmental factors, except pH values, and the macroinvertebrate abundances were \( \log(x + 1) \) transformed to approach a normal distribution (Legendre & Legendre, 1998). The analysis was performed with the ADE-4 software (Thioulouse et al., 1997).

Results

Environmental factors

Environmental factors showed spatial differences among sampling ponds and temporal differences among seasons (Table 1). The mean conductivity of ponds varied from 148 to 783 \( \mu \)s/cm (mean = 288 \( \pm \) 54 (S.E.) \( \mu \)s/cm, median = 243 \( \mu \)s/cm). The high conductivity at site 2 was probably due to the location of pond 2 which was near the coast. Low dissolved oxygen was found at all ponds (mean = 3.13 \( \pm \) 0.37 mg/l, median = 3.23 mg/l). This reflected the fact that these ponds were more or less affected by human activities due to their location. With the exception of pond 10 (pH = 6.84), all ponds possessed pH values above 7.0. All ponds had mean water temperature between 21.6 and 24.7\( ^\circ \)C with the lowest in winter (9.9\( ^\circ \)C at site 1–15.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 6) and the highest in summer (27.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 10–31.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 4). The mean depth of ponds ranged between 15.1 and 42.8 cm (mean = 29.1 \( \pm \) 3.0 cm, median = 30 cm). The sediment depth of ponds varied from 0.8 to 6.2 cm (mean = 2.18 \( \pm \) 0.47 cm, median = 1.6 cm).

Macroinvertebrate communities

In total, 31 macroinvertebrate taxa were recorded at the 11 sampling ponds during the sampling year (Table 2). In terms of taxon richness, pond fauna were dominated by Gastropoda, of which 10 taxa were recorded. Odonata were represented by nine taxa. Compared with Gastropoda and Odonata, Hemiptera (3 taxa), Hirudinea (2), Ephemeroptera (2), Decopoda (1), Coleoptera (1), Diptera (1), Oligochaeta (1), and Ostracoda (1) were relatively poor. For Diptera, Oligochaeta, and Ostracoda, it is likely to be an underestimate of the species-level diversity in these sampled ponds. The total macroinvertebrate species richness of ponds ranged between 2 and 13 (mean = 7.2 \( \pm \) 1.4 S.E.; median = 6) (Table 2). The abundance of B. melanostictus varied from 0 to 95.6% of total number of animals.
