Long-term stability of cladoceran assemblages in small, shallow, Canadian Shield lakes experiencing marked calcium declines L. E. Mosscrop1 · A. M. Paterson2 · A. M. DeSellas2 · J. Kurek3 · R. Weeber4 · J. P. Smol1 Received: 14 May 2014 / Accepted: 2 July 2015 / Published online: 17 July 2015 © Crown Copyright 2015 Abstract A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats, and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. Furthermore, recent water chemistry monitoring data show that shallow lakes in Ontario are sensitive and have responded significantly to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. Here, we use paleoecological techniques to examine cladoceran assemblages in modern and pre-industrial sediments of 30 shallow lakes to determine the key environmental gradients that influence present-day assemblages, and to assess how assemblage structure has changed since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s). Redundancy analysis of present-day cladoceran assemblages and key environmental variables identified lake surface area and Secchi depth as significant predictors of assemblage composition. In our data set, Secchi depth was not correlated to water clarity but rather to macrophyte cover, suggesting that cladoceran assemblages were highly influenced by habitat structure. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where pelagic cladoceran taxa have changed significantly in relative abundance over time, cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments of shallow lakes did not differ significantly in composition. While the specific reasons for this muted response are unknown, we hypothesize that: (1) littoral taxa may be less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability may vary spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. Keywords Canadian Shield · Calcium · Cladocera · Paleolimnology · Shallow lakes Introduction Long-term declines in calcium (Ca) concentrations have been identified as a significant threat to biological communities in softwater lakes within the Precambrian Shield (Jezierski et al. 2008). In relatively deep lakes, an ominous symptom of this “aquatic osteoporosis” is a decline in the relative abundances of keystone grazers, such as the Ca-sensitive cladoceran Daphnia pulex (Jezierski et al. 2008, 2015), as lake water Ca concentrations near a laboratory-determined threshold of approximately 1.5 mg/L (Ashforth and Yan 2008). These findings were recently confirmed in paleolimnological assessments of softwater, oligotrophic lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (DeSellas et al. 2011; Jezierski et al. 2012a, b), where changes in the composition of sedimentary cladoceran assemblages since pre-industrial times were generally consistent with declining calcium concentrations in relatively deep, thermally-stratified lakes. However, it is apparent that shallow and deeper lakes may respond differently to environmental stressors, because of greater interactions at the sediment–water interface, differences in nutrient cycling and availability, and enhanced coupling of the terrestrial environment with the littoral zone in shallow systems (Scheffer 2004), in addition to differing predation regimes (Wellborn et al. 1996). In shallow lakes, the sediment–water interface typically has a higher influence on water quality, aquatic macrophytes and other biota (Tessier and Woodruff 2002; Scheffer 2004), with greater sediment–water contact resulting in increased sediment re-suspension, turbidity, internal nutrient loading, and possibly planktonic productivity. Furthermore, environmental and substrate conditions within the littoral zone are often complex and highly heterogeneous, resulting in diverse assemblages of macro- and micro-flora and fauna. Despite their prevalence across the Boreal Shield, limnological data for shallow lakes in Ontario, Canada, are sparse relative to deeper lakes. Nevertheless, recent monitoring data from softwater, shallow lakes clearly show that they are sensitive, and have responded chemically to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. For example, the shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region (referred to as the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes) have declined by 26 % in lake water calcium concentrations, on average, since monitoring began in the 1980s (Jezierski et al. 2008). What is currently unknown, however, is whether or not these marked chemical changes have altered biological communities over time, as has been reported for deeper, dimictic lakes in the region. Recent work by Shapiera et al. (2011) has shown that some littoral microcrustacean taxa (i.e., Alona rectangula, Disparalona spp., Pleuroxis truncates, and Scapholebris rammneri) have Ca burdens comparable to Ca-rich daphniids, suggesting that some of the inhabitants of the littoral zone may be less competitive at low Ca concentrations. A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats (Minns et al. 2008), and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. In order to determine the dominant factors influencing cladoceran assemblages in shallow, Canadian Shield lakes, we examine long-term changes in sedimentary cladoceran assemblages in thirty shallow lakes in the Muskoka region of south-central Ontario [a subset of the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes noted in Jezierski et al. (2008)]. These lakes are relatively undisturbed by local watershed impacts (e.g., shoreline development, forestry operations), but are affected by regional stressors, such as climate change, acidification, and declines in lake water calcium levels. Using paleolimnological techniques, we ask: (1) What are the key environmental gradients that influence sedimentary cladoceran assemblages within these shallow lakes? (2) How does water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in these shallow lakes compare to those recorded by DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) in nearby, deeper, thermally-stratified lakes? and (3) How has cladoceran assemblage structure changed in these shallow lakes since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s)? Given the significant changes in water chemistry that have been observed in these shallow lakes over the past few decades (particularly long-term declines in lake Ca concentrations), we expect cladoceran assemblage structure to respond accordingly, as has been observed in nearby, deeper lakes (e.g., Jezierski et al. 2008). Specifically, we anticipate that the relative abundance of littoral taxa requiring higher levels of Ca will be lower in modern lake sediments. Materials and methods Study area and field sampling The thirty study lakes are located within relatively remote, boreal forests of the Canadian Shield in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (Fig. 1; Table 1). The lakes were chosen from a subset of lakes sampled by the Canadian Wildlife Service (CWS) as part of Environment Canada’s Acid Rain program, a biological monitoring program designed to assess the impacts of acidifying deposition on wildlife and their habitats in eastern Canada (McNicol et al. 1996). Lakes were selected for study from the CWS lake set if they were less than 7 m in maximum depth, and within 3 km of an accessible road. The region lies at the southern limit of the Boreal Ecozone, and forest composition ranges from predominantly coniferous to mixed hardwood. Conifer, mixed, and thicket swamps are the dominant peatland types. The lakes and watersheds are underlain by Precambrian granitic bedrock (Jeffries and Snyder 1983). The shallow and acidic soils are low in nutrients, with local deposits of clay, sand and gravel apparent in some of the watersheds (Chapman and Putnam 1984). Regional stressors affecting lakes in the area are derived, in part, from seasonal cottages, recreational activities associated with cottages, and infrastructure required by populations from organized towns and hamlets. However, the majority of the shallow lakes (27 of 30) included in this study do not have residences located within their local catchments. This area has an active forestry industry and it is likely that the majority of the catchments have been logged in the past, and several have active, selective tree-cutting programs that may have contributed to recent declines in lake water Ca concentrations (Watmough et al. 2003). Fig. 1 Map showing the location of the 30 study lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Water chemistry was collected on a regular basis between 1990 and 2009 by CWS, except for Heney Lake, which has been sampled by the Ontario Ministry of the Environment’s Dorset Environmental Science Centre (DESC; www.desc.ca) since 1979. Available water chemistry data include nutrients [total phosphorus (TP), Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN), nitrate + nitrite (NO_3/NO_2), ammonia (NH_3)], dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), major cations and anions [calcium (Ca), potassium (K), sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), sulphate (SO_4), conductivity (cond)], and measures of acidity [pH, Gran alkalinity (Alk)]. TN was calculated as the mass sum of TKN and NO_3/NO_2. Maximum lake depth (Zmax) was measured on site and lake area (ha) was provided by CWS. Secchi depth (cm), surface water temperature, and an estimate of relative macrophyte cover (%; available for 25 of the study lakes) were measured at the time of core collection (July 25 to August 12, 2011). Importantly, Secchi depth estimates were not a direct measure of water clarity in six of the study lakes, where the disc was obscured by dense macrophyte growth (lakes 1204, 1215, 1230, 1331, 1336, 1511). Relative macrophyte coverage (%) was assessed by dividing each lake into sections, estimating % macrophyte coverage within sections, and then averaging these estimates to produce a single, lakewide estimate. Glew (1989) sediment cores were sampled at the deepest point of each of the 30 study lakes in the summer of 2011. The cores were extruded on shore using a Glew (1988) vertical extruder and the top and bottom 2-cm of sediment was sectioned at 0.25-cm intervals. Bottom sediments were not collected from four of the lakes because core lengths were less than 4 cm. Bottom sediments were considered only if the core was longer than 15 cm, as previous dating of sediment cores from lakes in this region has reported the background time period (i.e., pre-1850) to fall between core depths of \( \sim 15 \) and 20 cm (Mills et al. 2009; Moss-crop 2013). Laboratory analyses Replicate microscope slides from the top and bottom samples from each of the 30 lakes were prepared for cladoceran analyses following techniques outlined in Korhola and Rautio (2001). Sediment was deflocculated in a 10 % KOH solution and heated at 80 °C for approximately 30 min. The sediment was then passed through a 37-μm sieve and rinsed with de-ionized water. The residue that was retained on the sieve was transferred to a small vial using de-ionized water. Two to three drops of ethanol were added to prevent fungal growth, and two to three drops of safranin-glycerin solution were added to stain the cladoceran remains. Finally, samples were mixed and 50-μl aliquots were pipetted on to slides, and permanent slides were made using glycerin jelly. Taxonomic identifications of fossil cladocerans followed Szeroczynska and Sarmaja-Korjonen (2007) and Korosi and Smol (2012a, b). Cladoceran remains were identified under 20× or 40× magnification (10× ocular lens) using a Leica DMRB light microscope with bright field optics. Slides were scanned in their entirety to ensure that all identifiable remains were counted. All cladoceran remains (e.g., carapaces, headshields and post-abdominal claws) were tabulated separately for each taxon. The most abundant remain was then used to calculate the number of individuals (Frey 1986). Usually 2–5 slides were sufficient to enumerate 100 individual cladocerans; however, five of the 30 lakes had low cladoceran counts (i.e., under 100 individuals), although above the recommended minimum of 70 individuals (Kurek et al. 2010a). Daphnia were separated into two groups based on postabdominal claw morphology [i.e., D. pulex complex (stout middle pectin) or D. longispina complex (uniform middle pectin); Korosi et al. (2011)]. Bosminids were not separated into individual species (i.e., Eubosmina and Bosmina longirostris) but were grouped as Bosmina spp. Statistical analyses Shallow lake set Principal components analysis (PCA: correlation matrix) was used to examine the variation in present-day water chemistry across lakes. Prior to statistical analyses, site 1503 was identified as an outlier, both chemically (>95 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of environmental data) and biologically (>90 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of cladoceran assemblage data), and thus removed from subsequent tests of the modern data. The shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region were last sampled by CWS for water chemistry in the autumns of 2007, 2008 or 2009 using a bottle grab sample from the surface waters. Although coring occurred in 2011, the 2007-09 water chemistry data were considered to be representative of present-day conditions, as water chemistry in regional lakes (Zmax: 5.8–38 m) has changed little over the past 3-5 years relative to changes that have occurred over the past three decades (Palmer et al. 2011). Environmental variables, with the exception of Alk, Secchi, pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, TN were either log (area, Zmax, cond, TP, NH3, SO4), square root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration, to stabilize variances in the data. Prior to statistical analyses, the cladoceran data were pre-screened for rare taxa. Cladoceran taxa that did not occur in at least two lakes with a relative abundance of at least 2 % were removed from further statistical analyses. Detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) on square-root transformed species data, with detrending by segments, was used to determine the amount of taxa turnover. Because of the short gradient lengths of the first DCA axis of species data (i.e. <2 SD units), linear ordination techniques (PCA and Redundancy Analysis, RDA) were used to: (1) examine the variation in present-day cladoceran assemblages across lakes; and (2) explore the relationships between cladoceran species and environmental data, and to select the minimum set of environmental variables that best described the distribution of species (ter Braak and Šmilauer 2002). For RDA, manual forward selection was used to determine significant (p < 0.05) environmental predictors. Assemblage similarities were calculated using the Bray-Curtis similarity coefficient (Bray and Curtis 1957) on square-root transformed species data, and used to construct a similarity matrix among modern (present-day) and pre-industrial sediment samples. Using this matrix, a one-way analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) was calculated to test for significant differences in cladoceran assemblage composition between modern and pre-industrial sediment samples using the Paleontological Statistics (PAST) program (v2.16; Hammer et al. 2001). Following ANOSIM, dominant cladoceran taxonomic groups (Bosmina spp, Chydoridae, Daphnia, Holopedium glacialis, and Macrothricidae) in pre-industrial (bottom) and modern (top) sediments were compared individually using a Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test with corrected p-values. Comparing water chemistry and cladoceran assemblages in the 30 shallow and 41 deeper lakes DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) studied current conditions and long-term changes in cladoceran assemblages in deeper and generally larger lakes within Muskoka-Haliburton. Because the cladocerans were processed and identified in the same lab using similar techniques, it was possible to compare water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in the surface sediments of the shallow and deeper lakes. Prior to comparison, the following adjustments were made to ensure taxonomic harmonization of Cladocera in the datasets: (1) Eubosmina and Bosmina were combined, because this taxonomic differentiation was not made in the shallow lake set; (2) Daphniids were combined into D. pulex (stout pecten) and D. longispina (uniform, fine pecten) complexes; (3) Sididae were combined; and (4) Macrothricidae were combined. Water chemistry was also simplified in the comparison of shallow and deeper lakes, as there were differences in the variables analysed. We included nutrients (TP, NO3/NO2), DIC, DOC, major cations and anions (Ca, K, Na, Mg, SO4, cond), pH, and lake morphometric variables (Zmax and lake surface area). Untransformed water chemistry variables from the shallow (n = 30) and deep (n = 41) lakes were compared in SigmaStat v3.1 using Mann–Whitney Rank Sum tests. For ordination analyses, environmental variables, with the exception of pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, were either log (x + 1) (area, Zmax, cond, TP, SO4), square-root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration. RDA with manual forward selection was run on the combined dataset (including both shallow and deeper lakes) to explore the relationship between cladoceran taxa and environmental data across the broader predictor gradients. Cladoceran assemblages in the present-day sediments of shallow and deeper lakes were also compared using ANOSIM, and the cladoceran taxa responsible for the observed differences in assemblage composition between the lake sets were identified using the statistical procedure Similarity Percentages (SIMPER; Clarke 1993). Results and discussion Lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario have recorded significant changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, including increases in DOC, declines in Ca concentrations, and declines in TP concentrations (Mallory et al. 1998; Jeziorski et al. 2008; Palmer et al. 2011). For some measures (e.g., Ca), the chemical changes observed in shallow lakes were larger than those recorded in nearby, deeper lakes (Jeziorski et al. 2008). However, despite changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, and significant changes in cladoceran assemblages observed in neighbouring, deeper lakes in south-central Ontario since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), we observed minimal change in cladoceran assemblages in a comparison of modern and pre-industrial sediments of thirty small, shallow lakes. Beginning with an exploration of present-day water chemistry and its relationship to modern cladoceran assemblages, we discuss our findings below, focussing first on the shallow lake dataset, and then combining these data with previously published cladoceran analyses from nearby, deeper lakes. Water chemistry in shallow lakes The first (\( \lambda = 0.36 \)) and second (\( \lambda = 0.21 \)) PCA axes captured 57 % of the variation in the water chemistry data from shallow lakes (Fig. 2). The first axis showed strong positive correlations with pH, Alk, Ca, Mg, specific conductance, and DIC. The second PCA axis was strongly positively correlated with lake surface area (ha), Secchi depth, and SO\(_4\), and showed weaker negative correlations with TP, TN and DOC. As reported in surveys from deeper lakes (Paterson et al. 2001; DeSellas et al. 2008), the first axis likely reflects natural variation in surficial geology, from more acidic sites with shallow soils to sites with thicker deposits of till. This, in turn, regulates the sensitivity of sites to acidic deposition, with PCA axis 1 separating dilute lakes with low buffering capacities (i.e., bottom left quadrant) from lakes with relatively higher ionic concentrations (Fig. 2). As reported in other regional surveys (e.g., Paterson et al. 2001; Kurek et al. 2010b), lake area was negatively correlated with nutrient (TN, TP) and DOC concentrations. In part, this may be related to differences in drainage ratios and lake volumes, with smaller, more productive lakes in the dataset receiving higher areal inputs of nutrients and DOC. Small, shallow lakes also have lower ratios of lake volume/sediment surface area, and thus may experience higher relative inputs of nutrients from lake sediments, particularly during periods of higher productivity (i.e., during the ice-free season) (Søndergaard et al. 2003), or during periods of higher water column stability. For plotting purposes, the environmental vectors have been multiplied by factors of 2 and 0.5 for the sites and species biplots, respectively For example, despite being shallow, some of the study lakes were stratified at the time of sampling (mid-summer), with observed differences in water temperature of more than 10 °C across the water column (Mossocrop 2013). Cladocera in the surface sediments of shallow lakes and their relationship to environmental variables In general, fossil cladocerans from both the surface (30 lakes) and pre-industrial (26 lakes) sediments of the shallow study lakes were well preserved and abundant, with the samples dominated by taxa of the families Bosminidae and Chydoridae. However, the uppermost 0–0.25 cm sediment interval had very few remains in most lakes (i.e., the top intervals were sampled conservatively in order to preserve the sediment–water interface, and contained little sediment after freeze drying), and therefore the 0.25–0.5 cm interval was used to represent modern conditions. Forty-five cladoceran taxa were identified in the surface sediments of the 30 shallow lakes, with 25 remaining for statistical analyses after removing rare taxa (Table 2). Bosmina spp. was the dominant taxon in the majority of the lakes, with a mean relative abundance of 42.7 %, and with relative abundances of more than 50 % in 16 of 30 lakes. However, four lakes (1204, 1503, 1506, 1537) had less than 10 % abundance of Bosmina spp., which tends to be a rare occurrence in larger, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008; Kurek et al. 2010b). Forward selection in RDA identified two environmental variables (Secchi depth and lake surface area) that explained significant (p = 0.005) amounts of variation in the cladoceran data (Fig. 3). When constrained to these variables, the first two RDA axes explained 20 % of the variation in the cladoceran species data, although most of the explained variation was loaded onto RDA Axis 1. In the shallow lake dataset, with the exception of a weak relationship with NO3/NO2, Secchi depth was not significantly correlated to any other water chemistry variable, despite showing strong correlations with DOC, colour, and nutrient concentrations in deeper lakes (e.g., Pérez-Fuentetaja et al. 1999). This may be because Secchi depth measurements were obscured by dense macrophyte beds in six lakes, and so was not a true measure of water clarity across the lakes. Thus, as reported in other studies of shallow lakes (e.g., Chambers and Kalff 1985; Cheruvelil and Soranno 2008), Secchi depth serves as a reasonable surrogate for percent macrophyte coverage in our dataset (Fig. 4a), reflecting differences in habitat structure among lakes. Many littoral and benthic Cladocera are influenced by macrophyte density (Tremel et al. 2000; Yarwood-Buchanan 2005; Declerck et al. 2011), and our results confirm that habitat structure is an important predictor of sedimentary cladoceran composition in shallow lakes (<7 m) in south-central Ontario. For example, Bosmina spp. were found generally at higher relative abundances in larger lakes with fewer macrophytes, whereas members of the Fig. 4 Scatterplots showing the relationship between: a percent macrophyte cover and Secchi depth; and PCA Axis 1 scores of sedimentary cladoceran remains and Secchi depth (b), for shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Chydoridae were more prevalent in the smaller, macrophyte-rich lakes (Fig. 3). A comparison of the main direction of variation in the modern cladoceran assemblage (PCA Axis 1 sample scores of the species data) with Secchi depth showed a significant linear relationship, suggesting that Secchi depth, and thus macrophyte cover (Fig. 4a), tracked an important direction of variation in the fossil cladoceran data (Fig. 4b). It is worth noting that our results differ from a recent survey of littoral microcrustacean assemblages from 22 Canadian Shield lakes in south-central Ontario. Walseng et al. (2008) examined the relative importance of acidity and habitat structure as regulators of littoral microcrustacean assemblage composition, as previous studies had reported the importance of both as predictors (e.g., acidity: Walseng et al. 2001; Hann and Turner 2000; e.g., habitat structure: Tremel et al. 2000). In their survey, Walseng et al. (2008) found little difference in assemblage composition in wave-washed sandy habitats versus more protected habitats dominated by floating-leaved macrophytes. Furthermore, lake water pH was found to be strongly correlated with the main direction of variation in the species data (Walseng et al. 2008). The apparent discrepancy in the above studies and our results likely stems from the much narrower chemical gradient examined in our study lakes (e.g., our study, pH 5.4–6.1; Walseng et al. 2008, pH 4.6–6.9), and our more general definition of habitat structure (low to high macrophyte cover). As described below (‘Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes’), we found that water chemistry increased in importance as a predictor of cladoceran assemblage composition when the chemical gradient was broadened, as was the case when we combined our shallow lake data with those from 41 deeper lakes. Similarly, in a survey of cladoceran assemblages from the surface sediments of 50 moderately deep (mean Zmax = 10.6 m) Boreal Shield lakes in northwestern Ontario, water chemistry and lake surface area explained the largest amount of unique variation in the data set (Kurek et al. 2011). Cladoceran assemblages in top–bottom paleolimnological assessments of shallow lakes The cladoceran assemblages recorded in the modern and pre-industrial sediment samples were not significantly different (Fig. 5; ANOSIM, R = 0.01, p = 0.22, n = 26), with Bosmina spp. the dominant taxon in both time periods. Univariate analyses of the dominant taxa showed that only the Macrothricidae, which in these lakes included Acantholeberis curvirostris and Ophryoxus gracilis, were significantly different (i.e., lower in relative abundance in the modern samples) in modern and pre-industrial sediments (p < 0.05). Members of this family are generally considered to be tolerant of lower ionic concentrations and more acidic conditions (Fryer 1980; Walseng et al. 2003) and, as scraper feeders, commonly live in close association with macrophytes (Elmoor-Loureiro 2007). However, these are conditions that describe many of the lakes currently, and so the decrease in Macrothricidae over time cannot easily be explained by these general ecological characteristics. The other most common cladoceran groups, including littoral taxa, did not change significantly from pre-industrial to modern times (p > 0.05), when examined across all lakes. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where significant changes in cladoceran assemblages have been observed since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), species composition in shallow lakes was remarkably stable in a comparison of present-day and pre-industrial sediments. In the deeper lakes, changes were linked to the interactive effects of several environmental stressors, resulting in long-term changes in water chemistry. Specifically, decreases in the relative abundance of pelagic, Daphnia Fig. 5 Comparison of the relative abundances of the dominant cladoceran taxa in modern and pre-industrial sediments from 26 lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada. Modern and pre-industrial cladoceran relative abundances are shown as solid and open bars, respectively spp. that require more Ca were related to declines in lake water Ca concentrations, a finding supported by laboratory evidence (Ashforth and Yan 2008), field data (Cairns 2010), and other paleoecological studies in the Muskoka-Haliburton region (Jeziorski et al. 2008, 2012a, b). Similarly, Shapiera et al. (2011) demonstrated that several littoral microcrustacean taxa differ in their Ca content, as shown for Daphnia spp. (Jeziorski and Yan 2006), suggesting littoral cladoceran composition may be sensitive to changes in Ca levels. However, the lack of change in littoral taxa, despite low lake water Ca concentrations and evidence of declining Ca over time, may indicate that: (1) littoral taxa are less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed, or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability varies spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. The observed differences in the biological response in shallow and deep lakes may also be influenced by other factors, such as a differential response of lakes of varying depths to climatic change. For example, dimictic lakes in south-central Ontario have increased in thermal stability since the 1980s (Palmer et al. 2014), and mixing depths have become shallower because of climate-driven increases in dissolved organic carbon concentrations (Keller 2007). Daphniids, in particular, have been shown to be sensitive to increases in lake water temperatures, and an increased growing season with warming may provide some taxa with an advantage over macroinvertebrate predators, such as Chaoborus (Neill 1981). However, in a recent assessment of long-term trends in zooplankton in Dorset, Ontario lakes (Yan et al. 2008), changes in mean cladoceran body size (the strongest trend) were unrelated to changes in climate indices, and Sweetman et al. (2008) reported no consistent change in planktonic cladoceran communities (bosminids and daphniids) in a top–bottom paleolimnological study of 50 lakes from central Canada, a region that has warmed considerably over the last century. Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes Despite similarities in trends over time (e.g., for Ca, Jeziorski et al. 2008), a comparison of modern water chemistry from shallow and nearby, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008) revealed many significant differences (Fig. 6, Table 3). In general, shallow lakes are smaller, of lower ionic content, and higher in DOC concentrations. The shallow and deeper lakes did not differ significantly in TP concentrations, but NO3/NO2 concentrations were significantly lower in the shallow lakes at the time of sampling (October). Presumably, this was due to its rapid uptake by phytoplankton and periphytic algal communities at the end of the growing season, and because of higher denitrification rates in the more productive shallow lake systems (Søndergaard et al. 2005). Of interest to our study were differences in Ca concentrations, which were significantly lower in the shallow lakes (Fig. 6; Table 3). Although the specific reasons for this difference need to be explored further, lake water Ca concentrations reflect a balance of inputs and losses, with the primary input coming from exchangeable soil sites within the watershed (Houle et al. 2006). It is likely that the smaller, shallow lakes also have smaller catchment areas that are less likely to contain deeper soils, resulting in lower areal export of Ca to surface waters. Furthermore, selective tree-cutting programs in these catchments may have further lowered Ca concentrations through the removal of this Ca pool from the watershed, and its accelerated uptake during forest regrowth (Watmough et al. 2003). Finally, the uptake of calcium by macrophytes in the shallow lakes may also contribute to lower ambient Ca levels, particularly at the end of the growing season, prior to senescence. The combined data set of shallow and deep lakes extended the gradients of all physical and water chemistry variables. As a result, RDA identified lake surface area, maximum depth, Ca, Mg, and SO4 as variables explaining the main direction of variation in the cladoceran assemblage data (Fig. 7). RDA Axis 1 clearly separated the small, shallow lakes from the larger, deeper lakes examined by DeSellas et al. (2008). A closer examination of the data showed that certain pelagic taxa, such as Daphnia (both the D. pulex and D. longispina complexes), were rarely found in the shallow lakes (on average only 2 % relative abundance). Larger Daphnia species, for example, may experience reduced predation pressure in deeper lakes with vertical diel migration (Jeppesen et al. 1997). In support of this hypothesis, the separation of assemblages based on lake depth occurred at approximately 7 m (Fig. 8), a depth which broadly distinguishes dimictic from polymictic lakes in the region, acknowledging variation associated with differences in local topography, lake fetch and DOC concentrations (colour). This finding is consistent with an earlier study from the region (Jeziorski et al. 2012b) that identified 6 metres as an important depth threshold for cladoceran species composition. These results were confirmed by ANOSIM, where cladoceran assemblages recorded in the surface sediments of deeper and shallow lakes differed significantly (ANOSIM, R = 0.59, p = 0.001), with SIMPER analysis showing that nine taxa contributed to \( \sim 80\ \% \) of the dissimilarity between assemblages in deep and shallow lakes (Table 4). Three pelagic taxa (Bosmina spp., D. pulex complex and Daphnia longispina complex) contributed to more than half of the dissimilarity (Table 4), occurring in higher relative abundances in the deeper lakes, again reflecting the clear separation of assemblages based on lake depth and corresponding habitat dominance of either the pelagic or littoral zone (Fig. 8). Conclusions In an examination of cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments from thirty shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, we found modern cladoceran assemblages to be highly influenced by habitat structure. Secchi depth (related to macrophyte cover) and lake area were shown to be important predictors of assemblage composition in lakes <7 m in depth. A top–bottom paleolimnological analyses revealed that cladoceran assemblage structure was relatively stable through time in the shallow lakes, despite significant changes in our water chemistry data over the last few decades. These results suggest that littoral Cladocera are less influenced by changes in water chemistry than pelagic taxa, including significant declines in Ca concentrations, a surprising result given the variation that exists among littoral taxa in Ca content (Shapiera et al. 2011), and evidence of significant biological change having occurred in nearby, deeper lakes. Further analyses on continuous sedimentary records are recommended to confirm these patterns through time, and to obtain additional information on changes in water quality and biological condition in shallow lakes in the region. These analyses should include an examination of other palaeoecological indicators (e.g., diatoms; sedimentary chlorophyll \( a \)) to reconstruct long-term changes in water quality and ecological condition. Laboratory analyses Replicate microscope slides from the top and bottom samples from each of the 30 lakes were prepared for cladoceran analyses following techniques outlined in Korhola and Rautio (2001). Sediment was deflocculated in a 10 % KOH solution and heated at 80 °C for approximately 30 min. The sediment was then passed through a 37-μm sieve and rinsed with de-ionized water. The residue that was retained on the sieve was transferred to a small vial using de-ionized water. Two to three drops of ethanol were added to prevent fungal growth, and two to three drops of safranin-glycerin solution were added to stain the cladoceran remains. Finally, samples were mixed and 50-μl aliquots were pipetted on to slides, and permanent slides were made using glycerin jelly. Taxonomic identifications of fossil cladocerans followed Szeroczynska and Sarmaja-Korjonen (2007) and Korosi and Smol (2012a, b). Cladoceran remains were identified under 20× or 40× magnification (10× ocular lens) using a Leica DMRB light microscope with bright field optics. Slides were scanned in their entirety to ensure that all identifiable remains were counted. All cladoceran remains (e.g., carapaces, headshields and post-abdominal claws) were tabulated separately for each taxon. The most abundant remain was then used to calculate the number of individuals (Frey 1986). Usually 2–5 slides were sufficient to enumerate 100 individual cladocerans; however, five of the 30 lakes had low cladoceran counts (i.e., under 100 individuals), although above the recommended minimum of 70 individuals (Kurek et al. 2010a). Daphnia were separated into two groups based on postabdominal claw morphology [i.e., D. pulex complex (stout middle pectin) or D. longispina complex (uniform middle pectin); Korosi et al. (2011)]. Bosminids were not separated into individual species (i.e., Eubosmina and Bosmina longirostris) but were grouped as Bosmina spp.

Measurements of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton using ethanol as extraction solvent By ANNE-METTE JESPERSEN and KIRSTEN CHRISTOFFERSEN With 2 figures and 4 tables in the text Abstract The use of ethanol as extraction solvent for the determination of chlorophyll-a was evaluated on a variety of cultures and natural populations of phytoplankton. Ethanol was equally efficient as methanol in the extraction of chlorophyll-a from cultures or natural populations of phytoplankton. An extraction period of 6 hours in cold ethanol was in most cases sufficient to complete the extraction, but longer extraction time or heating the solvent may be necessary when green algae dominate the plankton. The extraction efficiency decreases 10—25 %, when water reduced the ethanol concentration from 96 % to 83.5 %. Interference from chlorophyll-b in the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol comprised 3—9 % and should be ignored in routine determinations of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton. Introduction Measurement of the chlorophyll-a content in phytoplankton is often used as an index for biomass, which is an important parameter in many ecological studies in aquatic environments. Since Strickland & Parsons published a procedure in 1968 involving extraction in 90 % acetone a large number of methodological changes have been published. Despite the fact that acetone is still commonly used in many marine studies, it is now recognised, that the extraction efficiency is low in the presence of many green and bluegreen algae (Marker 1972, Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Riemann & Ernst 1982), which are commonly found in eutrophic lakes and coastal marine environments. As an alternative, alcoholic extraction solvents have been proposed. Holm-Hansen & Riemann (1978) concluded that methanol was a fast and efficient extraction solvent, but it has been criticized because of its unhealthy characteristics (Nusch & Palme 1980). Ethanol was introduced several years ago (Nusch & Palme 1975), but the extent to which calibrations and evaluations have been carried out is still limited. However, some studies (Moed & Hallegraef 1978, Nusch 1980, Arvola 1981) have demonstrated that the extraction efficiency of ethanol is comparable to that obtained by methanol. The Danish Standardization Council recently has chosen ethanol as the Danish Standard (DS 1985) and this solvent may emerge as the general extraction solvent for both freshwater and marine environments. The aim of this work was to evaluate (1) the extraction efficiency of hot and cold ethanol using a variety of phytoplankton cultures and natural populations, (2) the effect of water content in the solvent, and (3) the interference of chlorophyll-b on the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a. Materials and methods Water samples were collected from 12 different lakes situated in the central part of Jutland and North Zealand (Denmark) from september to december 1983. Phytoplankton primary productivity and the algal composition of the lakes are listed in Table 1. Surface water samples were collected in 5-litre plastic bottles, and subsamples were filtered through Whatman GF/C (47 mm) filters using a vacuum pressure of approximately 20 cm Hg. The filters were sucked dry and stored at −20 °C prior to use. The algae composition was determined from water samples fixed with Lugols iodine. Phytoplankton cultures included Scenedesmus quadricauda (Brebisson), Chlorella vulgaris (Beijerinck), Selenastrum capricornutum (Printz) and Pediastrum duplex (Meyen), grown in a modified Österlind B medium (Steemann Nielsen & Wiium-Andersen 1970), in a 12/12 hours light and dark cycle at 25 °C. Light source was a Phillips LTD 18w/84 and light intensity was 260 \( \mu \)E m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\). The growth conditions of the culture were checked from cell counts using a haemocytometer. Aliquots of cultures in log or stationary phases were filtered through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) at 20 cm Hg and used immediately. Filters containing phytoplankton cultures and natural phytoplankton were extracted in 5 ml of either 96 % ethanol or absolute methanol. In one experiment, ethanol concentrations from 96 % to 83.5 % were used. Table 1. Dominating species and annual phytoplankton primary productivity from the 12 Danish lakes studied.

In another experiment, 96 % ethanol were heated to 70 °C (in water bath) for 2—6 minutes, otherwise "cold" (20 °C) ethanol were used. Extraction time varied from 6 to 24 hours. All samples were measured spectrophotometrically after refiltering the pigment extract through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) as described in Riemann & Ernst (1982). A Beckmann 26 spectrophotometer was used (1 cm cuvettes). Maximum absorbance in the red region of the spectrum was at 665 nm for chlorophyll-a in absolute methanol and 96 % ethanol. Corrections for turbidity were made by subtracting the absorbance at 750 nm which never exceeded 5 % of the 665 nm measurements. Maximum absorbance for chlorophyll-b was at 650 nm and 652 nm in ethanol and methanol, respectively. The following specific absorption coefficients were applied: chlorophyll-a in ethanol 83.4 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965), in methanol 77.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) cm (Riemann 1978), and chlorophyll-b in ethanol 45.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965). Reproducibility of the chlorophyll measurements was tested using two phytoplankton cultures and one natural phytoplankton population. The coefficient of variation ranged from 1.7 % to 7.8 % (n = 10). Analysis of data were performed using Student t-test and two-factor analysis of variance (P < 0.05). Results and discussion The extraction efficiency of ethanol Two experiments were set up to compare the extraction efficiencies of ethanol and methanol. In the first experiment, four species of green algae and one natural population of phytoplankton were extracted for 6 hours in 96 % ethanol and absolute methanol. In addition, the pigments were extracted in hot and cold ethanol for various times. Except for Scenedesmus and Chlorella in stationary phases, no significant differences were found in the amount of chlorophyll-a extracted from any of the cultures, regardless solvent, heating procedure or length of extraction period (Fig. 1A—D). Furthermore, no significant differences were observed between the methanol, cold and hot ethanol extractions in the natural population of phytoplankton (Fig. 1 E). The chlorophyll-a extracted from Scenedesmus after 6 hours using hot ethanol was 54 % higher than after 6 hours methanol extraction (Fig. 1F). No significant differences were observed after 6 hours using methanol and cold ethanol, but the chlorophyll-a concentration in cold ethanol increased during the extraction period, and after 24 hours the chlorophyll concentration was 46 % higher, compared with the results obtained from methanol extraction. There were no significant differences between the extracted chlorophyll-a concentrations after 18 hours in cold and hot ethanol. Assuming that 6 hours is a sufficient extraction period using methanol (Riemann & Ernst 1982), the results obtained from Chlorella (in log phase), Selenastrum, Pediastrum and the natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø suggested a complete extraction after 6 hours in cold Fig. 1 A—F. Chlorophyll-a (mg l^{-1}) extracted from various algae cultures using absolute methanol for 6 hours or 96% cold and hot ethanol for 6, 12, 18 and 24 hours. Chlorella vulgaris was extracted during both stationary and exponential growth phase, Selenastrum capricornutum, Pediastrum duplex, and Scenedesmus quadricauda during exponential growth phase. The sample after 12 hours extraction using Pediastrum was lost. Black columns represent methanol, white columns cold ethanol, and hatched columns hot ethanol extrations (n = 3). Bars represent standard deviations. ethanol. In contrast, methanol extraction of Scenedesmus was not efficient enough to remove chlorophyll-a from the cells, since hot ethanol gave more chlorophyll-a than the cold solvents. In a similar experiment Nusch (1980) reported that methanol and ethanol were equally efficient and always more efficient than acetone. This is in contradiction to the results reported by Arvola (1981), who found that methanol was superior to ethanol. Riemann & Ernst (1982) demonstrated that methanol extracted more chlorophyll-a from Scenedesmus acutus compared with ethanol extractions. Thus, extraction efficiencies for the various solvents may be species specific. According to our results a 6 hour extraction in cold ethanol, without further treatment, is sufficient to complete the extraction in most cases. When certain green algae are dominating, longer extraction time or heating the solvents may be necessary. In a second experiment, the extraction efficiency of cold ethanol was compared with methanol extraction on natural populations of phytoplankton, to investigate the influence of phytoplankton composition on the extraction efficiency. Based on the first experiment, an 18 hour extraction time was chosen. No significant differences were found between the results obtained from ethanol or methanol extractions (Table 2), except in the samples from Ellesø and Thorsø. In Ellesø, 7% more chlorophyll was extracted with ethanol than with methanol, and in Thorsø the methanol extraction gave 3% more chlorophyll than the ethanol extraction. Table 2. To investigate the influence of temperature on the extraction efficiency, samples from 6 different lakes were heated for 2 to 6 minutes and the results were compared with results obtained from cold ethanol extraction (Table 3). The hot ethanol extractions were generally more efficient than the cold ethanol, but no significant differences were found except from Skanderborg Lillesø, where 10—15 % more chlorophyll was obtained by heating for 2 to 6 minutes, and from Ellesø after 4 minutes. The results from the natural populations of phytoplankton support the conclusion that cold ethanol is an equally efficient extraction solvent as methanol. In the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø, which was totally dominated by *Scenedesmus*, more chlorophyll was obtained by heating the solvent. It is known from the literature that different treatments such as homogenization, ultrasonic treatments and heating (Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Nusch 1980, Riemann & Ernst 1982) optimize the extraction conditions, especially when algae belonging to Chlorophyceae and Cyanophyceae dominate. However, the pigment concentration in the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø was extremely high and this may have reduced the extraction efficiency and furthermore caused an increased amount of water in the solvent, which also result in reduced extraction efficiency (see below). The effect of water content in the extraction solvent The effect of water in the ethanol was tested on *Chlorella, Scenedesmus* and on a natural population of phytoplankton. When distilled water was passed through GF/C filters during the standard procedure, the retained water was 0.139 ml (SD = 0.006; n = 3) on 25 mm GF/C filters, and 0.396 ml (SD = 0.003; n = 3) on 47 mm GF/C filters. This increased water content resulted in a 3—7 % reduction in the ethanol concentration. Based on these data, ethanol concentrations between 83.5 % and 96 % were tested. Fig. 2 A—C. Chlorophyll-a (mg l\(^{-1}\)) extracted from *Chlorella vulgaris*, *Scenedesmus quadricauda* and a natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø, using varying percentages of ethanol (diluted with distilled water). Bars represent standard deviations (n = 3). When the ethanol concentration was reduced from 96% to 83.5%, 10% less chlorophyll was extracted from *Chlorella*, 14% less from the natural population of phytoplankton, and 25% less from *Scenedesmus* (Fig. 2). The relative large reduction in chlorophyll extracted from *Scenedesmus* is probably related to its morphology, which increases the possibility of water adhesion to the cells. Furthermore, the results in Fig. 2 are underestimated, since the true water content on filters containing algae, bacteria, and detritus is higher than those predicted from experiments using distilled water. Previous findings have demonstrated that the extraction efficiencies in methanol (Rie- MANN 1980) and ethanol (NUSCH 1980), were reduced when the water content was increased. Thus, the water content in ethanol extraction should be kept as low as possible. Spectrophotometric interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol Pigment extracts from natural populations of phytoplankton often contain chlorophyll-b and -c, which have absorption maxima close to that of chlorophyll-a in the red region of the spectrum. The interference from chlorophyll-b leads to an overestimation of chlorophyll-a, while the interference of chlorophyll-c in most cases may be ignored, since the absorption maximum of chlorophyll-c is 30—35 nm from the absorption peak of chlorophyll-a (MARKER et al. 1980). To investigate the interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol, the absorption at 665 nm was read at different mixed solutions of the two pigments (Table 4). When chlorophyll-b constituted from 5 % to 100 % of the chlorophyll-a (by weight), the absorbance at 665 nm increased from 1.5 % to 35.1 %. In similar experiments using methanol RIEMANN (1978) found an 1.4 % to 44.6 % overestimation, when chlorophyll-b constituted 5 % to 90 % of the chlorophyll-a content. This interference is higher than for ethanol, because the maximum absorbance of chlorophyll-b is closer to the peak of chlorophyll-a in methanol. LOFTUS & CARPENTER (1971) reported, that chlorophyll-b rarely constituted more than 10—20 % of the chlorophyll-a content in natural populations of phytoplankton, dominated by green algae or other algae containing chlorophyll-b. Only in one sample they found 40 % chlorophyll-b. RIEMANN & ERNST (1982) investigated six green algae and found, after optimal extraction, that chlorophyll-b constituted 13—33 % of the chlorophyll-a in methanol extracts. Table 4. Assuming that chlorophyll-b will constitute at most 30% of chlorophyll-a in natural populations of phytoplankton, the maximum interference of chlorophyll-b leads to an 9.3% overestimation of chlorophyll-a in ethanol. To correct for this interference involves either 1) a detailed spectrophotometric determination at different wavelengths (Strickland & Parsons 1972), or 2) a chromatographic separation of the chlorophylls. The first method is not recommended (Marker et al. 1980) because chlorophyll-a thereby is overestimated and a chromatographic separation is still not applicable in routine measurements. As a consequence, it is suggested that interference from chlorophyll-b in ethanol extracts may be ignored when chlorophyll-a is determined from phytoplankton. Measuring the trophic status of ponds: Relationships between summer rate of periphytic net primary productivity and water physico-chemistry Lionel Sager* Laboratory of Ecology and Aquatic Biology (LEBA), University of Geneva, Chemin des Clochettes 18, CH-1206 Geneva, Switzerland ARTICLE INFO Article history: Received 2 July 2008 Received in revised form 22 December 2008 Accepted 23 December 2008 Published online 3 January 2009 Keywords: AFDW Alternative stable states Assessment Eutrophication Nitrogen Phosphorus Submerged macrophytes ABSTRACT The monitoring of the water quality is a major environmental concern and specific method of assessment needs to be addressed for ponds. Among threats on freshwater, eutrophication remains an important and widespread problem. To assess if the trophic state of ponds can be significantly predicted by physico-chemical surrogates, parallel measurements of water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) were performed on a set of nine lowland Swiss ponds representing the whole spectrum of trophic states. The developed methods to measure periphytic NPP on artificial substrates give similar values between the pseudo-replicates and are functional for ponds. The winter concentration of total nitrogen (TN) in the water is a significant predictor of the average summer rates of NPP while in submerged macrophyte beds total phosphorus (TP) is a better predictor. Rates of NPP measured in open water were most often higher and water transparency lower than in macrophyte beds, highlighting the positive influence of macrophytes on water quality and a possible co-occurrence in a pond of contrasting conditions when submerged species are present. This emphasizes the importance of maintaining or restoring submerged macrophyte stands in ponds to improve the water quality. 1. Introduction Monitoring and quality improvement of surface freshwater are major environmental concerns worldwide (Johnson et al., 2001). In European countries, the Water Framework Directive (WFD, Council of the European Communities, 2000) provides clear objectives to obtain at least a good qualitative and quantitative status of all waters in Europe by 2015. To attain these goals, all the aquatic compartments have to be considered and assessed with specific methods to classify them into high, good, moderate, bad and poor ecological quality. As ponds are recognized as distinct aquatic compartments from rivers and lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2005a) and react in a different manner to impacts, specific methods are required for their assessment; some are currently being developed (Menetrey et al., 2005) or are already operational (Biggs et al., 2000; Boix et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2005), review in Indermuehle et al. (2005). Moreover, recent works have established ponds as being very significant components of the freshwater resource, in terms of their contribution to both local and regional biodiversity (Murphy, 2002; Oertli et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2003), confirming their importance to the concept of integrated catchments management. Practically, however, ponds are neglected in the implementation of the WFD as many countries have set a lower size limit of 50 ha to apply the directive on water bodies (Nicolet et al., 2007). Among the current threat on freshwater, eutrophication through diffuse pollution from agriculture (Havens et al., 2001) remain as an important, widespread and even growing problem for freshwater and coastal oceans (Carpenter et al., 1999; Bronmark and Hansson, 2002; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003; Craft et al., 2007). Accelerated rates of eutrophication linked to human activities have generated much interest during the last decades and many studies have been carried out, particularly in large lakes and rivers. Notably, an international research program of OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) associated ranges of quantifiable environmental parameters to each of 5 classes of trophic state (ultra-oligotrophic, oligotrophic, mesotrophic, eutrophic, hypertrophic) that were previously attributed with an expert system to 100 northern temperate lakes. To implement the WFD in Danish lakes, Sondergaard et al. (2005b) proposed a pre-classification of lakes based on their trophic status given by the concentration of total phosphorus (TP), in order to identify biological indicators of eutrophication. Focusing on the assessment of eutrophication, one must take into account that high nutrient concentration in small lakes or ponds do not necessarily bring a high phytoplankton biomass and a turbid water as observed in larger lakes (Sondergaard et al., 2005a), because other controlling factors are implicated including a possible scale effect (Schindler, 1998). In this way, the ranges of concentrations of nutrients in the water assigned by OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) to each trophic class for lakes are not necessarily valid for ponds. Eutrophication is historically described as a regular increase of the phytoplankton primary productivity following larger inputs of inorganic nutrients (Naumann, 1927). This emphasis that any classification of water bodies in trophic state is an artificial reading of a continuous biological process. This continuity in eutrophication process complicates the establishment of well-defined limits between classes and furthermore the assignment of biological indicators values to a trophic state (Sondergaard et al., 2005b). As already pointed out by Rodhe (1969), the trophic state is expressed by a rate and must be determined by measuring primary production. Thus measuring rates of primary production in ponds varying in water concentration of major nutrients would permit to determine which parameters are best correlated and best predictors of the measured production and so eutrophication, even if these parameters are not the only factors determining the primary productivity as early underlined by Naumann (1932). Additionally, eutrophication is coupled at least in lakes by a shift from the dominance of benthic to pelagic production (Sand-Jensen and Borum, 1991; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003). As the rate of primary productivity can be spatially and temporally heterogeneous for a given water body (Liboriussen and Jeppesen, 2006), a simple physico-chemical surrogate valid for ponds would be very valuable for ecological assessment. To record primary productivity in ponds varying in trophic status, the chosen method must be standardized and usable on the full range of trophic conditions. Ponds have generally a high littoral surface area relative to their pelagic volume and therefore an important potential for macrophyte and periphyton growth (Wetzel, 1990). For that reason, the benthic contribution to primary production can be more important in shallow systems like ponds than in deep lakes. Taking this benthic fraction into account is of prime importance, particularly for oligotrophic systems where it can represent the majority of the primary production (Vadeboncoeur et al., 2002). In addition, measuring periphytic productivity rather than macrophyte biomass could be more pertinent as the development of submerged vegetation is known to be discontinuous along trophic gradients (Scheffer, 1990). Moreover, Smoot et al. (1998) have shown that on artificial substrate the response of periphyton growth to nutrients is similar to the response of phytoplankton, making periphyton a valuable descriptor of phytoplankton response. This property allows the use of this indicator on the full spectrum of trophic conditions as it can grow in ponds with oligotrophic to hypertrophic conditions, where planktonic algae become the main producers and replace the benthic fraction. To focus on water quality, submerged macrophytes have the capacity to link the sediment with the overlying water and so to mobilize nutrients from the sediments (Graneli and Solander, 1988), in contrast to periphyton that cannot directly uptake nutrients stocked in the sediment (except for the epipelon (Hansson, 1992)). To standardize the measure of periphytic productivity, independent of the grazing pressure by zooplankton and macroinvertebrates, it has to be performed in controlled conditions with no access to grazers. Furthermore, the measurement must take into account the presence of macrophyte beds. Actually these can influence the abundance of periphyton by several mechanisms, notably competition for nutrient resources, release of allelopathic substances (Wium-Andersen, 1987; Ervin and Wetzel, 2003; Gross et al., 2003) or sheltering of the zooplanktonic and macroinvertebrate communities from predation (Timms and Brian, 1984; Jeppesen et al., 1997). Moreover, parallel measurements of periphytic productivity performed outside and inside beds of submerged plants permit to calculate a mean value of productivity between results obtained in open water and in macrophyte beds and also to detect potential co-occurrence within a pond of contrasting conditions linked by a continuous gradient between clear water zone colonized by submerged macrophytes and turbid zone without submerged vegetation. Co-occurring contrasting conditions have already been described by Scheffer et al. (1994) in shallow lakes of greater surfaces than the ponds considered here. Since there is an important nutrient recycling and rapid turnover in ponds and other shallow systems, water concentrations of nutrients show considerable fluctuation during the growing season, and a large part are mobilized in the biota and are not measurable in the water. During winter however, for ponds located at medium and high latitude, biological activity and primary productivity are very low and nutrients are in the water column for the most part, in dissolved or particle forms (Linton and Goulder, 2000). Hansson (1992) notably observed the peak of total phosphorus (TP) in open water occurring during winter for high latitudes lakes. Thus, winter values are expected to give a better picture of the potential of primary productivity by quantifying the amounts available in spring for the growth of producers. Furthermore, winter values avoid the confounding effects of uptake of phosphorus and denitrification that occur with summer readings (James et al., 2005). By performing parallel measurements of winter water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic productivity on a small dataset of ponds, this study aims to: 1) identify correlations between periphytic productivity and physico-chemical indicators of the trophic state, 2) detect a possible co-occurrence of contrasting conditions of turbidity and periphytic productivity in a given pond, 3) assess if a single chemical surrogate of primary productivity can potentially be used to classify ponds in the same biogeographic area according to their trophic state. Such a surrogate could serve as a basis to calibrate ecological value by species and select biological metrics of eutrophication. Additionally, this study will provide an opportunity to test the reliability of the method adapted for measuring the periphytic net primary productivity in ponds. 2. Material and methods 2.1. Study sites This study took place in the western part of the Swiss Plateau, a distinct biogeographic area (sensus Gonseth et al., 2001). The landscape of this area, where human population and agriculture are concentrated, has been intensely modified during the 20th century by increase in urbanisation and the intensification of agricultural practices (Lundstrom-Gillieron and Schlaepfer, 2003), resulting in the fragmentation of natural areas. The nine permanent ponds surveyed for this analysis represent a gradient of primary productivity from oligomesotrophic to hypertrophic. These ponds, located between 420 and 773 m a.s.l, are small and shallow, ranging from 327 to 10,616 m^2 in surface area, (mean: 3087 m^2, median: 2733 m^2) and from 0.38 to 1.03 m in mean depths (mean and median: 0.7 m). All these sites are colonized by fish. Four of the nine water bodies are colonized by submerged species of macrophytes (S), three by floating-leaves species (F) but without submerged hydrophytes and two supports only emerged vegetation (E). The location and the main morphometric characteristics of the ponds are given in Fig. 1 and Table 1. The sampling of the vegetation was made with the standardized method of Oertli et al. (2005) and consists of prospection by square quadrats (0.25 m^2) disposed equidistantly along transects perpendicular to the longest axis of the pond and located at regular intervals according to the pond size. The minimum number of quadrat prospected per pond (n) is related to the water surface area (m^2) by the equation \( n = 1.96 - 2.8 \times \log_{10}(\text{area}) + 2.6 \times (\log_{10}(\text{area}))^2 \). Such a strategy was shown to sample at least 70% of the real richness. A specie list was noted for each quadrat along with abundance in semi-quantitative classes. The number of quadrats prospected and the main species of macrophytes by site are given in Table 2 along with an estimation of their abundance at the pond scale. ![Map showing the study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds.](page_1092_186_1017_670.png) Fig. 1 – Study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds. 2.2. Periphytic primary productivity Rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) on artificial substrates and in absence of herbivores (method adapted from Clesceri et al., 1998; Chase, 2003) were directly recorded in situ in each pond as a measure of periphytic primary productivity at two points chosen with criterion detailed thereafter. All measures were performed at location with similar water depths (0.8 m) and in areas with minimal shading from terrestrial vegetation or from surrounding plants for measures in macrophyte beds. In all cases the shading at the location of the measurement point never attain five percent of the surface. Measurements were performed continuously from June 6, 2005 to August 2, 2005, across the period of longest daytime in northern hemisphere and until the aquatic vegetation biomass summer peak (Jackson et al., 1994). This period correspond to the time of optimal growth conditions for periphyton on artificial substrate as identified by Jobgen et al. (2004). Submerged macrophyte presence in four ponds and floating-leaves species presence in three ponds were taken into account by measuring productivity inside vegetation stands and in open water. Growth rates were determined by measuring the accumulation of periphyton on the inner side of transparent plastic boxes (polystyrene PS) offering each a colonisable surface of 0.023 m^2 (Fig. 2). Boxes were covered by a net on their open face (mesh size 0.25 mm) to prevent, or at least limit the income of grazers, and were positioned two to three centimeters below the water surface in groups of three pseudo-replicates fixed around a pole planted in the pond base. According to Chase and Ryberg (2004), such a mesh retains about 10% of the available light “but did not significantly reduce algal growth in a controlled experiment performed in the absence of grazers”. Preventing the access of grazers is of prime importance for this study and as Jones et al. (2002) pointed out, the grazing pressure is a stronger limiting factor of the net production of periphyton than the water nutrient concentration. To reduce to the minimum meteorologically related variation among ponds, sampling and replacement of the boxes of all nine ponds were carried out over the shortest possible time period (two days). 2.3. Physico-chemistry Water physico-chemistry was measured once in winter and physical parameters were measured five times in summer (at each box replacement). The winter fieldwork was undertaken during three consecutive days (from 9 to 11 February, 2005) after a long frost period. Water sampling and field measurements were made at the deeper central point of each pond by drilling a hole in the ice cover. Water samples were taken at 20 cm below the icy surface with a sampling bottle, and then stocked in acid pre-rinse PE plastic bottles immediately before being stored in the dark in a refrigerated box. Water samples for the analysis of dissolved components (PO₄-P (soluble reactive phosphorus = SRP), NO₃-N, NH₃-N) were filtered in situ trough 0.45 μm filters (Schleicher & Schuell ME 25). Unfiltered samples were kept for total phosphorus (TP) and total nitrogen (TN) analyses. All samples were stored in the dark at 4 °C and analysed within 48 h after field collection. The SESA water quality laboratory (VD) analyzed all the water samples with standard methods. TP was determined after potassium persulphate digestion at 121 °C and under pressure for half an hour; SRP was further measured by the ascorbate acid/molybdenum blue method (Clesceri et al., 1998). TN was determined by chemiluminescence after oxidization in NO at high temperature and reaction with ozone. NH₃-N was determined by colorimetry with the salicylate method. NO₃-N was determined by ion chromatography. A deep profile was made in the field for physical parameters (temperature, pH, conductivity) using a multi-parameters probe (YSI 556®, YSI Incorporated, Yellowspring, USA). Water turbidity (NTU) and transparency (cm) were also measured in the field with a turbidity meter (WTW Turb 355 IR®, WTW GmbH, Weilheim, D) and a Snellen tube of 60 cm length. 2.4. Data analyses To assess the reliability of the primary productivity measurement method, mean rate of productivity and variance were calculated for each measurement point and sampling occasion. In parallel, productivity rates by pseudo-replicates were box-plotted by point and sampling occasion to visually detect eventual outliers. To test if any measured physical and chemical variables could explain the differences of periphytic productivity among ponds, multiple stepwise linear regressions were performed (threshold of entry \( p \leq 0.05 \), removal \( \geq 0.1 \)). As we wanted to explore the relationships between summer periphytic growth rate and winter concentrations of TP or TN, linear stepwise regressions were performed with these two parameters in a first set of predictors and physical parameters in a second set to see if their inclusion could improve the \( R^2 \) and significance of the models. Regressions were performed between seasonal productivity rates of each pond and the corresponding mean of physical parameters of the water as well as winter concentrations of nutrients. Mean productivity rate by pond is the sum of the means of the two sampling points of each sampling occasion. To refine the regressions according to the sampling points, the same above procedure was applied separately for three subsets of the data (open water (O), submerged species (S) and floating-leaves species (F)). As one of the ponds shows very high rates of productivity, we reapplied the whole procedure after removing this extreme value from the dataset to verify if the identified regressions remained significant. The critical \( \alpha \) values were corrected by applying the Bonferroni corrections for non-independent comparisons (Maxwell and Delaney, 1990). As a second objective we wanted to compare the rates of periphytic productivity between sampling points located in the same pond, respectively inside versus outside macrophyte stands. With all sampling occasions, there were enough data to test the significance of the differences among locations with an unparametric test (Mann–Whitney) between productivity by boxes at the sampling points. As there were not enough pseudo-replicates to validate the statistical test by sampling occasion, simple box plot by sampling points and by sampling occasion were plotted for each pond. This revealed if differences were detectable, and helped rank productivity rates at each vegetated sampling point in space and time as lower, equal or higher to unvegetated points. 3. Results The set of ponds display a wide range of periphytic growth rate, nutrient concentrations and water physical parameters. Measures of periphytic growth rate by single point and sampling occasion ranged from 0.022 to 48.406 gC/m²/14 days (0.0016–3.458 gC/m²/day) and the mean seasonal value for ponds ranged from 1.284 to 52.950 gC/m²/56 days (0.023– 0.946 gC/m²/day). The daily mean seasonal value by point and by pond and the mean value by point and by sampling occasions are given in Table 3 along with variance between pseudo-replicates, except for the first sampling occasions where the three boxes by point were weighted together. Rates for the last sampling occasion in open water of pond P3 could not be retained for the analyses because the boxes emerged during sampling. Six exposed boxes were also damaged and the measurements were removed from the dataset. Winter nutrient concentrations of TP ranged from 0.002 to 0.346 mg L⁻¹ and TN varied from 0.7 to 5.83 mg L⁻¹. Ranges and mean values for summer and winter measurements of physico-chemical parameters are given in Table 4 3.1. Regressions of productivity rates with physico-chemical parameters The mean seasonal rates of periphytic primary productivity by pond defined as the sum of the mean value by pond for each sampling occasion are positively correlated to the water concentration of total nitrogen (TN) measured during the previous winter (linear regression for the whole season, Table 5, model 1, \( r^2 = 0.974, p = 8.55e-07 \)). With the stepwise procedure, the regression remained the same with winter TN as unique predictor. Without the extreme value of the hypertrophic site (P6), the regression between the seasonal productivity by pond and the winter concentration of TN remained valid, even if less significant and less strong (model 2, Table 5, \( r^2 = 0.754, p = 5.16e-03 \)). In that case, the stepwise regression retained the mean water transparency as second predictor negatively correlated with productivity, improving the performance of the model (model 3, Table 5). The scatter plot of the seasonal values of productivity versus TN or TP presented in Fig. 3 shows additionally the OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982; Wetzel, 1983; Forsberg and Ryding, 1980) limits of nutrient concentration between trophic classes as well as the limits between the classes of ecological quality included for shallow lakes by Sondergaard et al. (2005b). For the measures located in open water, regressions with TN were also significant for seasonal productivity (model 1, Table 6, \( r^2 = 0.937, p = 1.68e-05 \)). The stepwise procedure even improves the model by including the mean turbidity as second predictor (model 2 Table 6). Without the upper value of productivity (pond P6), the regressions are less strong but the predictors remain the same.

Effects of floating-leaved macrophytes In the three ponds supporting floating-leaved plant stands, there was no particular trend when comparing productivity rates measured in open water and within stands. Productivity rates were very similar between location at the two sites colonized by Polygonum amphibium (P1 and P2), and on the remaining site (P8), rates in macrophyte stands were higher at first, but then lower than in open water even if the stands remained stable over the eight weeks of measurement. 4. Discussion 4.1. Reliability and limitations of the method for ponds The rates of productivity measured for each pseudo-replicate for a given point and sampling occasion were similar even if the variance between the boxes increased for high means (see Table 3 and Fig. 4). Despite this uncontrolled effect, the method is sensitive and allows classifying ponds of this dataset by trophic states characterized by TN as a higher variance between pseudo-replicates occurs in systems already hypertrophic. However as the data material is small and restricted to a limited geographic area, these results need to be confirmed on a broader scale to generalize this outcome for ponds in the area. Observed rates (Table 3) were low compared with other studies (for instance see Chase (2003) with measured productivity ranging between 6.12 and 56.2 g/m²/day). This could be due to the smaller net mesh size used to cover the open face of boxes, which could have limited the colonization by algae. On the other hand this net allowed inter-sites comparisons by strongly reducing and homogenising the residual grazing factor. The nature of the artificial substrate can also be involved. Actually, the review of Cattaneo and Amireault (1992) suggested that the type of artificial substrate is not crucial but Danilov and Ekelund (2001) observed no growth of periphyton on PVC substrate and the formation of a slim layer of bacteria covering the artificial substrate. No such layer was observed in the current study and the poly-styrene plastic often employed in biology, notably for the Petri dishes, is more likely to have played an inhibitory effect as it seems to be the case with PVC. 4.2. Periphytic productivity and nutrients The significant positive regression observed between TN and mean periphytic growth rate is consistent with other studies, for instance Luttenton and Lowe (2006) found significant correlation between nitrogen concentration on nutrient-diffusive substrata (NDS) and total biovolume of periphyton growing on this substrate. Similarly Chase and Ryberg (2004) found positive correlations between primary productivity measured with a method similar to this study and TP and TN in order of importance. Kahlert and Pettersson (2002) also measured an increase in the biomass of benthic algae with trophic levels even if it was not correlated with the nutrient status of the algae itself.
