submerged_macrophytes_as_refuges.full_text:
Submerged macrophytes as refuges for grazing Cladocera against fish predation: observations on seasonal changes in relation to macrophyte cover and predation pressure Julia H. Stansfield¹, Martin R. Perrow²*, Louise D. Tench¹, Adrian J. D. Jowitt² & Ayesha A. L. Taylor¹ ¹National Rivers Authority, Biology Laboratory, Station Road, St Olaves, Great Yarmouth, NR31 9JA, UK ²ECON, School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich NR4 7TJ, UK (*author for correspondence) Key words: zooplankton, zooplanktivorous fish, macrophyte, refugia, predator/prey interactions, lake restoration Abstract The provision of a refuge from fish predation for large-bodied Cladocera among stands of submerged macrophytes is thought to be an important stabilising mechanism against nutrient-induced phytoplankton increases in clear water shallow lakes. The occurrence of any refuge effect in relation to the seasonal impact of both macrophyte development and recruitment of zooplanktivorous fish was monitored over the summer months (May to September) in three lakes (Cromes Broad, Hoveton Little Broad/Pound End, and Upton Broad) of variable trophic status, fish community structure and nature and extent of macrophyte cover, in the Norfolk Broads in Eastern England. At all sites, Daphnia spp. exhibited a early summer peak of abundance but had declined rapidly by July probably as a result of predation from underyearling fish. In extensive macrophyte stands (Cromes Broad) Daphnia spp. persisted after its elimination in open water, indicating some refuge effect. At sites with macrophyte cover and/or low fish predation pressure, Daphnia spp. was replaced by Ceriodaphnia spp., both with and without Simocephalus sp., thus maintaining large populations of grazing Cladocera, apparently capable of exerting a high grazing pressure on phytoplankton. This occurred, even under high predation pressure from a relatively high density of zooplanktivorous 0+ fish (Cromes Broad), consistent with the refuge hypothesis. In addition, at this site, significant positive associations of cladoceran abundance with increasing macrophyte cover were apparent throughout the summer. From information on the distribution of fish it is suggested that dense macrophytes offer the most suitable refuge through provision of predator-free space. Introduction Eutrophication of shallow freshwater lakes frequently results in increased standing crops of phytoplankton or perhaps filamentous algae. This in turn leads to the decline or loss of submerged macrophytes, typically through shading (Phillips et al., 1978; Scheffer, 1990), with consequent gross changes in biotic structure and function (Moss, 1983; De Nie, 1987; Bronmark & Weisner, 1992). However, there is growing empirical and experimental evidence that stabilising mechanisms associated with the presence of stands of macrophytes, may prevent or reduce increases in algal growth up to a threshold level of nutrient loading (Howard-Williams, 1981; Timms & Moss, 1984; Mitchell et al., 1988; Balls et al., 1989; Andersson et al., 1990; Blindlow et al., 1993; Van Donk et al., 1993; Schriver et al., 1995). Consequently, within a range of nutrient concentration, either macrophytes or phytoplankton may dominate; the alternative stable state hypothesis (Irvine et al., 1989; Scheffer et al., 1993). Several stabilising mechanisms which perpetuate the macrophyte-dominated state have been suggested. These include: allelopathy, the production of com- pounds limiting algal growth by the macrophytes themselves (Wium-Anderson et al., 1982); competition for N, with macrophytes maintaining a competitive advantage over algae through luxury uptake (Balls et al., 1989) and acting as a sink for available nutrients (in both water column and sediments) (Ozimek et al., 1990; Van Donk et al., 1993); prevention of resuspension of sediment and recirculation of fast sinking algae by wind and wave action through calming of the water column (James & Barko, 1990); provision of refuges for grazing zooplankton (Timms & Moss, 1984) and refuges for piscivorous fish acting upon the production (Spencer & King, 1984; Grimm & Backx, 1990) or the distribution (Werner et al., 1983; Persson & Eklov, 1995) of zooplanktivorous fish thereby reducing predation pressure upon the zooplankton (Hambright et al., 1986, Turner & Mittelbach, 1990). Detailed knowledge of the mechanisms responsible for maintaining clear water and low algal populations in lakes dominated by macrophytes is critical for those lake managers concerned with the sustainable restoration (i.e. reversal of anthropogenic eutrophication) of shallow lakes, particularly if this is to be achieved in a predictable and cost-effective manner (Shapiro, 1990). In restoration programmes, the refuge effect for zooplankton is particularly appealing (Shapiro, 1990). This is due to two reasons. First, after nutrient loading has been reduced to the range where macrophyte dominance is likely to be stable (TP<0.15 mg l\(^{-1}\) or higher if N is strongly limiting-Hosper & Jagtman, 1990; Jeppesen et al., 1990), the removal of zooplanktivorous fish, often termed biomanipulation (Lammens et al., 1990), is often required to enhance populations of grazing zooplankton to reduce algal crops to provide a suitable light climate for macrophyte growth. If this mechanism operates, then it is likely that grazing has some importance in maintaining clear water within macrophyte beds. Second, during the development of macrophyte stands following biomanipulation which may or may not be rapid (Meijer et al., 1994; Perrow et al., 1994, Moss et al., 1996), any stabilising mechanism is of increased value if it also preserves water clarity in the open water surrounding macrophyte stands. The diel migration of large-bodied Cladocera from macrophyte stands to open water to feed provides such a mechanism (Timms & Moss, 1984). Although macrophyte stands have been demonstrated to provide refuges for zooplankton (Schriver et al., 1995; Phillips et al., 1996) the timing of such effects relative to the seasonal development of macrophytes and recruitment of 0+ fish is poorly understood. The aim of this study was to describe the seasonal pattern of use of submerged macrophytes by grazing Cladocera in relation to potential predation pressure from fish and to determine whether the refuge effect is plausible as a mechanism in promoting clear water in beds of macrophytes. This adopted a comparative approach by monitoring zooplankton abundance and community structure, fish abundance and biomass, chlorophyll a concentration (as a index of algal abundance) and macrophyte cover during the macrophyte growing season (May–September) in three lakes of varying trophic status, fish community structure and nature and extent of macrophyte cover. Description of study sites The three lakes studied (Hoveton Little/Pound End, Crones and Upton Broads) are among the Norfolk Broads, a series (around 50) of small (1–124 ha), shallow (0.5–2 m) lakes in eastern England, formed from flooded medieval peat diggings. Most may now be classed as hypertrophic and only four retain their original macrophyte populations (Moss, 1983). The study sites represent a continuum from phytoplankton to macrophyte dominance. The first, Hoveton Little Broad, has been divided into two sections as part of a long term management strategy aimed at evaluating the effects of different restorative actions (Table 1). For the purposes of this study, Hoveton Little Broad, acts as a control section with turbid phytoplankton dominated water and few submerged macrophytes, whereas the other biomanipulated section, Pound End, has clear water and some macrophytes, although these are restricted to bird exclosures. The second, Crones Broad, retains a relatively high nutrient loading but has recently developed an extensive cover of Ceratophyllum demersum L. with Potamogeton freisii Rupr. (Perrow et al., 1997). The third, Upton Broad, being isolated from riverine inputs and surrounded by wet woodland, has largely retained its original character and has a large cover of macrophytes, particularly Najas marina L., with Chara spp., P. pectinatus L. and Zannichellia palustris L. Materials and methods Zooplankton, macrophytes and chlorophyll \( a \) Sampling for zooplankton, macrophytes, and chlorophyll \( a \) was carried out monthly from May to September 1994. At each site, ten zooplankton samples were taken from both open water and from amongst submerged macrophytes, where present. Where macrophytes occurred the density in a 0.25 m\(^2\) quadrat centred on each sampling point was expressed as PVI (per cent volume infested-Canfield et al., 1984). This was estimated by multiplying the estimated % cover by the height of the stand and dividing by the depth of water. At Pound End, five samples were taken from each of the two large (a. 500–1000 m\(^2\)) bird exclosures. In the open water and when macrophyte stands reached the water surface, a tube sampler was used (length 90 cm, diameter 10 cm) in order to sample the whole water column. When macrophyte stands did not reach the water surface a Patalas sampler (10 litre capacity) was used to obtain a sample from among the macrophyte stand. Water was strained through a 64 \( \mu \)m net and the animals retained were preserved in 70% alcohol. Samples were counted under a stereo microscope using 25 \( \times \) magnification. Differences between mean abundance of important cladoceran zooplankton between open water and macrophytes were tested using Mann-Whitney U-tests on each sampling occasion. In addition, the relationships between abundance of particular cladoceran species and % macrophyte cover were explored using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (\( r_s \)). Chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations were determined according to the methods of Moss et al. (1986). Fish Fish populations were sampled on two occasions, in May and September. This corresponded to the period prior to the recruitment of cyprinids and after the late summer period in which 0+ fish are likely to exert a depressive effect on zooplankton (Townsend & Perrow, 1989), respectively. In addition, sampling in May provided a baseline of the adult fish stock prior to the recruitment of underyearlings, whereas sampling in September allowed the relative recruitment strength of the 0+ fish to be estimated. Point abundance sampling (PAS) (Copp & Penáz, 1988) conducted with high frequency (600 Hz) pulsed DC electrofishing equipment was used to sample all habitats in proportion to their abundance. During sampling the 3 m fibreglass dinghy, with one electrofishing operator and one person controlling the boat using ‘push’ (facing the direction of travel) rowing, was rowed systematically along transect lines (8–10 oar strokes apart). At the equivalent distance along the transect line, a point was sampled by rapidly immers- ing the large (45 cm diameter) anode and swinging it through a 2 m arc in one motion. Any stunned fish were removed and transferred to individual buckets. The area sampled was quantified as 2.4 m\(^2\). This was achieved by using a voltmeter to determine the distance at which the voltage gradient was reduced to 0.12 V which may be used as the threshold limit for effective electrofishing (Copp & Penáz, 1988). At the end of each transect all fish were identified, counted, measured to the nearest mm fork length and weighed to the nearest gram, before being returned to a stretch of water that had been sampled previously. In addition, the % of the water column occupied by submerged macrophytes was estimated visually at each sampling point. The entire area of Pound End, Upton and Cromes Broads were sampled, whereas only part of Hoveton Little Broad (c. 6 ha-comparable to the size of Pound End) was covered. Results Fish The spring biomass of adult cyprinid and percid fishes was variable but low (up to 110 kg ha\(^{-1}\) but typically <15 kg ha\(^{-1}\)) (Table 2). The increase in biomass and especially, density, of potentially zooplanktivorous fish (all except pike, *Esox lucius* L. and eel, *Anguilla anguilla* (L.)) over the sampling period underlines the important contribution the recruitment of 0+ fish makes to fish production in the study lakes (Table 2). The relative recruitment strength of the different species in the different lakes is illustrated in Figure 1. Zooplankton Three genera of large-bodied grazing Cladocera zooplankton were found at significant density (>50 l\(^{-1}\)) in some or all of the study sites. These were *Daphnia hyalina/longispina* (Leydig/O.F.M.) *Ceriodaphnia reticulata/quadrangula* (Jurine/O.F. M.) and *Simocephalus vetulus* (O.F.M.). *Daphnia* spp. had an early summer peak of abundance, albeit of varying magnitude, at all sites, but had declined to low populations by July. At Cromes Broad, where extensive macrophyte stands developed from June onwards (Figure 1), *Daphnia* spp. persisted amongst the macrophytes after its elimination in open water (Figure 2). At Cromes and Pound End *Daphnia* spp. was replaced by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. both with (Cromes and Pound End) and without (Upton) *Simocephalus* sp., thus maintaining large populations of grazing Cladocera. This was not the case in Hoveton Little Broad, where cladoceran populations remained extremely low throughout the summer. The patterns of habitat use by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. varied between the different sites (Figure 2). At Pound End, macrophyte beds were favoured in early season, although once populations had built up by mid-summer, significant numbers (>100 l\(^{-1}\)) were found in open water. At Upton, prior to the peak in macrophyte populations, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was more abundant in open water, thereafter there was no significant difference between the different habitats. In contrast, in Cromes, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds compared to open water on all occasions (Figure 2). A similar pattern was shown by *Simocephalus* sp. where it occurred, as it was virtually always significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds (Figure 2). For sites with macrophytes, the relationships between PVI and the abundance of the different genera as well as all grazing Cladocera combined are shown in Table 3. At Cromes, there is a consistent pattern of increasing abundance of all genera, including *Daphnia* spp. while it was still present, with increasing PVI. At Upton no such pattern was found, with either no significant relationships, or in July, a significant negative relationship with *Ceriodaphnia* spp. Pound End represented an intermediate situation, with different species exerting different preferences: *Daphnia* spp. tended to be negatively associated with macrophytes; *Ceriodaphnia* spp. displayed positive associations early in the summer but no relationship in subsequent samples and *Simocephalus* sp. showed significant positive correlations with PVI on all occasions. Discussion Seasonal interactions between macrophytes, fish, zooplankton and phytoplankton There is clearly some interaction between extent of macrophyte development, intensity of predation by 0+ fish measured simply as a function of density and the structure and abundance of the cladoceran community and its potential impact on algal abundance (measured as chlorophyll *a*) (Figure 1). Indeed, where fish recruitment is poor or absent, *Daphnia* spp. populations typically persist throughout the summer months (Perrow et al., 1994). Conversely, it is clear that the relatively low overwintering stock of older fish exerted little influence on the development of the *Daphnia* spp. population. Second, in all sites, *Daphnia* spp. was quickly replaced by high densities of other species which is not consistent with food limitation and indeed at no site was the abundance of edible algae (expressed as chlorophyll *a*) apparently limiting. It therefore seems reasonable to conclude that predation by 0+ fish is responsible for the decline in *Daphnia* spp. Moreover, this appears to be readily achieved by a relatively low number of 0+ fish in Upton (prior to the development of macrophytes) and relatively moderate recruitment in Pound End and Hoveton Little Broads. However, *Daphnia* spp. persisted in Cromes Broad for a further month even in the presence of a suite of zooplanktivorous fish at relatively high density. This seems related to the early development of an extensive cover of macrophytes at this site. *Daphnia* spp. showed a positive association with macrophytes (Figure 2) and increasing macrophyte cover (Table 3) at this time, quite unlike the situation in any other site. Such use of macrophytes is consistent with the refuge hypothesis. However, *Daphnia* spp. appeared unable to exploit macrophytes as a refuge over an extensive period. This is in keeping with the behavioural ecology of the group which are typically pelagic and have been shown to avoid macrophytes (Pennak, 1973; Dorgelo & Heykoop, 1985). Recent experiments in the laboratory have shown that a clear trade-off exists, *Daphnia magna* Straus preferring to stay in open water until exposed to the risk of predation from zooplanktivorous fish whereupon it migrates to macrophytes, predation risk clearly outweighing repellency (Lauridsen & Lodge, 1996). However, many common fish species, particularly 0+ cyprinids, are capable of feeding in darkness (Townsend & Risebrow, 1982) and so the risk of predation, although reduced, is still evident. In addition, Daphnia spp. populations may suffer some predation from the fish concentrated in a low density of macrophytes (Figure 3). Therefore, in the face of intense predation pressure from a high density of zooplanktivorous fish, as at Cromes Broad, Daphnia spp. may not be able to persist through time, even with the provision of suitable refuges. Following the decline of Daphnia spp., at those sites retaining at least some macrophyte cover Ceriodaphnia spp. dominated, both with (Pound End) and without Simocephalus sp. (Upton). At Pound End, there was even some partial recovery of Daphnia populations in late summer. In contrast, the connected Hoveton Little Broad, with relatively high numbers of 0+ roach, displayed no replacement of Daphnia spp. with other species or any recovery of populations. The consequence of the presence of Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus was the maintenance of large populations (typically >50 l\(^{-1}\), Figure 1) of grazing Cladocera throughout the summer months in Cromes and Pound End. The patterns of habitat use of these species also appeared to be related to the potential predation pressure from fish, thus also consistent with the refuge hypothesis. For example, where predation pressure was presumably low from a low density of 0+ perch as in Upton, Ceriodaphnia spp. was present in both open water and macrophyte beds (Figure 2). Under moderate fish predation pressure in Pound End (0.45 m\(^{-2}\) of 0+ perch and roach), Ceriodaphnia spp. and particularly Simocephalus sp. were more abundant in macrophytes, although Ceriodaphnia spp. also occurred at high density in open water (Figure 2). In contrast, where predation pressure was likely to be intense from a suite of 0+ fish at high density (0.8 m\(^{-2}\)) in Cromes, large populations of both Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. were only maintained through association with macrophytes. Furthermore, under intense predation pressure the abundance of cladocerans was almost always positively correlated with increasing PVI suggesting that increasing cover offered a better refuge (Table 3). What is the mechanism behind the refuge effect? Schriver et al. (1995) demonstrate that a refuge effect may exist at low macrophyte density (15–20% of volume) but that this is dependent on fish density. However, the situation at Pound End suggests that even where the distribution of macrophytes is limited, providing patches of dense macrophytes are available (Table 1), a refuge against moderate predation pressure may be provided. The reasons for this may be that dense macrophyte stands contain relatively few fish (Figure 3). By implication, this suggests that predation risk for Cladocera declines with increasing macrophyte cover. Evidence for this is provided by Phillips et al. (1996), who demonstrated that predation pressure, derived from known numbers of fish with known diet, upon zooplankton declined with increasing macrophyte cover. It is therefore suggested that the formation of predator-free space is the mechanism responsible for the refuge effect. The question is, why do zooplanktivorous fish avoid dense macrophytes? (Engel, 1988). Several plausible mechanisms exist. First, oxygen concentrations (Davis, 1975) and pH (Beklioglu & Moss, 1995) may be unsuitable in macrophyte stands, although there is no evidence that either was limiting in the samples collected during routine monitoring of the study sites. Second, and perhaps more applicable, the foraging efficiency of some fish may decline with increasing habitat complexity (Winfield, 1986; Diehl, 1988). However, when foraging on zooplankton, this is clearly species and size dependent. For example, 0+ perch (Perca fluviatilis L.) may show high feeding efficiency in structured environments unlike 0+ roach (Rutilus rutilus (L.)) (Winfield, 1986), and vegetation may serve as a competitive refuge for perch (Persson, 1993). In support of this, several authors (Hall & Werner 1977; Carpenter et al., 1987; Venugopal & Winfield, 1993) have demonstrated that small fish may associate with macrophytes. However, this is typically a behavioural response to potential predation risk (Savino & Stein, 1982; Werner et al., 1983; Persson & Eklov, 1995) and not because of enhanced foraging opportunity. Whether small fish take refuge in macrophytes in response to predation risk is dependent on a number of factors including the functional type of predator and prey (Jacobsen et al., 1997). It is perhaps significant that in this study the relative proportion of piscivorous pike increased with increasing macrophyte cover (Figure 3). In addition, the individuals present in these habitats were 0+, the size class most likely to consume 0+ zooplanktivores (Van Densen, 1994). Therefore, a third explanation for the avoidance of dense macrophytes by fish in this study may be that they were exposed to a greater risk of predation in these habitats. This in turn may have led to a reduced predation risk for zooplankton (Turner & Mittelbach, 1990) thereby enhancing the refuge effect. Are refuging Cladocera able to control phytoplankton populations? The presence of large numbers of cladoceran grazers exerting an influence on phytoplankton populations is essential to the value of any refuge effect in explaining the presence of clear water in macrophyte-dominated lakes. Particularly to species other than Daphnia spp.? The relationship between grazing rate and body length are very similar for Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. compared to Daphnia spp. (Peters & Downing, 1984; Knoechel & Holtby, 1986; Bern, 1987; Mourelatos & Lacroix, 1990) and if at high enough density it seems reasonable to conclude that these species may be able to graze out phytoplankton crops, as observed by Turner & Mittelbach (1992). The interconnected Pound End and Hoveton Little Broads, with the same nutrient concentration, but radically different chlorophyll \(a\) values, appear to provide a convincing example of the grazing potential of these Cladocera (Figure 1). Moreover, in Cromes Broad, the filtering capacity of Simocephalus spp. and Ceriodaphnia spp., which are maintained at densities in excess of 50 l\(^{-1}\) throughout the summer months, appears to more than compensate for that of Daphnia spp. (Table 4). In Upton, the situation is less clear, where Simocephalus sp. is absent and the filtering rate of Ceriodaphnia spp. in midsummer does not compensate the loss of Daphnia spp. However, it is still comparable with that of Daphnia spp. at Cromes in early season, before the development of macrophytes when the only likely explanation for the control of phytoplankton populations is grazing. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that grazing by Ceriodaphnia spp. is at least a contributory factor in limiting phytoplankton development in Upton in mid- to late summer. From the patterns of habitat use of Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp., it is likely that only Ceriodaphnia spp. may have the potential to graze in the open water between stands of macrophytes, Simocephalus sp. always being limited to the macrophytes themselves (Lauridsen et al., in press). Thus in developing macrophyte populations at the beginning of the growing season or following a restoration attempt using control of zooplanktivorous fish, it seems that large populations of Daphnia spp. are required to provide the clear water necessary for macrophyte development. Following the establishment of macrophyte cover and/or recruitment of 0+ fish, Daphnia may be expected to decline, with Ceriodaphnia assuming the role of grazing in open water between as well as within macrophyte stands, with Simocephalus contributing to control of phytoplankton standing crop in the macrophyte beds themselves (Table 4). Conclusions Several results of the study are consistent with the refuge hypothesis: • The elimination of Daphnia spp. by 0+ fish is delayed where extensive stands of macrophytes are present in early summer. • Large populations (\(>50\ l^{-1}\)) of grazing Cladocera may be maintained throughout the summer at relatively high fish density. • The level of use of macrophyte stands is linked to fish predation pressure. • Cladoceran abundance is positively associated with increasing macrophyte cover. Essential to the value of the refuge effect as a mechanism promoting the stability of submerged macrophyte populations in shallow lakes, the presence of significant populations of grazing Cladocera seems to contribute to the maintenance of a low phytoplankton standing crop and the attainment of clear water. Moreover, macrophyte-associated species such as Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. appear to make an important contribution to this effect where Daphnia spp. is reduced by fish predation and/or disfavoured by extensive macrophyte cover. The mechanism for the refuge effect in this study appears to be the provision of predator-free space as zooplanktivorous fish appear to avoid dense macrophytes. Materials and methods Zooplankton, macrophytes and chlorophyll \( a \) Sampling for zooplankton, macrophytes, and chlorophyll \( a \) was carried out monthly from May to September 1994. At each site, ten zooplankton samples were taken from both open water and from amongst submerged macrophytes, where present. Where macrophytes occurred the density in a 0.25 m\(^2\) quadrat centred on each sampling point was expressed as PVI (per cent volume infested-Canfield et al., 1984). This was estimated by multiplying the estimated % cover by the height of the stand and dividing by the depth of water. At Pound End, five samples were taken from each of the two large (a. 500–1000 m\(^2\)) bird exclosures. In the open water and when macrophyte stands reached the water surface, a tube sampler was used (length 90 cm, diameter 10 cm) in order to sample the whole water column. When macrophyte stands did not reach the water surface a Patalas sampler (10 litre capacity) was used to obtain a sample from among the macrophyte stand. Water was strained through a 64 \( \mu \)m net and the animals retained were preserved in 70% alcohol. Samples were counted under a stereo microscope using 25 \( \times \) magnification. Differences between mean abundance of important cladoceran zooplankton between open water and macrophytes were tested using Mann-Whitney U-tests on each sampling occasion. In addition, the relationships between abundance of particular cladoceran species and % macrophyte cover were explored using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (\( r_s \)). The diversity of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte communities in ponds LAURIE E. FRIDAY Department of Biological Sciences, University of Exeter SUMMARY. 1. The range of factors which may influence the wide variation in the structure of pond communities is reviewed. 2. Factors explaining the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte taxa are investigated, using multiple regression analysis, for a group of ponds in which biogeographical effects are likely to be minimal. 3. Numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa in these ponds are highly correlated with pH and probably, therefore, with other associated aspects of water chemistry. 4. Many invertebrate taxa, from species to entire phyla, were not found below pH 5.5, but few characteristically 'acidophilic' taxa were apparent. 5. Details of species composition of the macroinvertebrate fauna differ widely even between ponds of similar pH. 6. The diversity and composition of macrophyte communities are not adequately predicted by any of the factors investigated. Introduction Ponds and other small water bodies are highly individual habitats: the fauna and flora usually vary widely, and often unpredictably, between ponds even within a small geographical area. While it is sometimes possible to find correlations between observed faunal or floral diversity and various factors, it is rarely possible, except by rigorous experimental treatment, to establish the causes of inter-pond variation. A wide variety of explanatory factors has been put forward, as a result of field studies of small water bodies or on theoretical grounds, as possible influences on the diversity and composition of pond communities. These factors may be grouped together under two broad headings: 'biogeographical' factors, operating via the dispersal of organisms to essentially insular habitats, and 'habitat' characteristics, both physico-chemical and biotic, influencing the establishment and persistence of colonizing species. These categories are not mutually exclusive, but form a useful basis for reviewing the wide range of factors which might explain inter-pond variation in the number and identities of species. Correspondence: Dr L. E. Friday, Department of Applied Biology, Pembroke Street, Cambridge CB2 3DX. (i) Biogeographical factors (a) Pond age. Studies of the initial colonization of newly created ponds show a general increase in the numbers of species of invertebrates and macrophytes (Gates, 1927; Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). Where dispersal distances are short, the rate of acquisition of new species has been observed to decline within a few years (Barnes, 1983), suggesting an approach to an 'equilibrium number of species', as predicted by MacArthur & Wilson's (1967) theory of island biogeography. However, Godwin's (1923) observations on the flora of much older ponds suggest that numbers of less vagile species (i.e. those with weak or passive dispersal) may continue to rise over many decades. As a pond ages, so the habitat it presents to colonists changes, partly due to increases in the extent and diversity of aquatic vegetation and in the production of autochthonous detritus. These changes are accompanied by changes in the identity of the dominant invertebrate taxa (Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). While it is possible to fit a model to the observed rise in numbers of taxa with age, the order in which individual colonists establish is not easy to predict. Invasion by an individual species depends on the availability of suitable propagules in 'source' habitats, the species' dispersal mechanisms, and the distance over which it has to disperse, but is also subject to chance (Talling, 1951). (b) Isolation. MacArthur & Wilson's model predicts a decrease in the equilibrium number of species on an island, and changes in the species represented, with increasing isolation from the source of colonists. Aho (1978a) found a significant correlation between isolation of small, productive Finnish lakes and the diversity of their molluscan faunas. Several authors have suggested that changes in isolation over historical or geological time (due to flooding, changes in river courses, creation or destruction of source habitats) have influenced the diversity of less vagile organisms in lakes (e.g. Boycott, 1919; Godwin, 1923; Aho, 1978b; Barbour & Brown, 1974). The immediate surroundings of ponds may also influence their chances of discovery by actively dispersing organisms, but surrounding vegetation and land use are likely to be of greater importance in their effect on aspects of the pond habitat, namely hydrology, water chemistry and allochthonous organic inputs. (c) Pond area. Connor & McCoy (1979), in their review of the species–area relationship, point out that the possible effects of area on community diversity have both biogeographical and biotic elements: as area increases, so the number of habitat types, with their associated species, is likely to increase; population sizes should also increase with area, thus reducing the extinction rate of resident species (MacArthur & Wilson, 1967); and large 'target' areas may simply receive a larger number of colonizing propagules, and therefore a chance of a greater variety of species, than smaller ones. Lassen (1975), Aho (1978a), Driver (1977) and Fryer (1985) found correlations between area (or log area) and the numbers of species of molluscs, chironomids and crustaceans respectively. Which of these aspects may account for the observed relationships is not possible to determine from diversity data alone, but Fryer (1985) suggests that the types of habitats found in different sized water bodies ('pond' as opposed to 'lake' habitats) may partly explain the composition of the crustacean faunas in his study area. Area, as an expression of the size of a water body, is also related to its persistence. Small ponds tend to be less permanent than larger ones, may show greater fluctuations in physical and chemical conditions, and so present quite a different type of habitat. Macan (1954, 1962) discusses the probable influence of habitat stability on the identity, and possibly on the diversity, of corixid species in a water body. (ii) Characteristics of the habitat (a) Habitat diversity. Factors contributing to the diversity of habitat for pond macrophytes include details of the bank topography and changes in substratum associated with irregularities in the shoreline. For the macroinvertebrate fauna, the diversity of macrophytic vegetation and local changes in substratum may be major factors. Observations by several authors on invertebrate communities associated with different species of macrophytes (e.g. Soszka, 1975; Dvorak & Best, 1982; Lodge, 1985), suggest that a correlation might be expected between macrophyte and macroinvertebrate numbers of species. Palmer (1981) found a close relationship between macrophyte species diversity and the number of species of Coleoptera and Hemiptera in a survey of base-rich ponds in Norfolk. (b) Competition and predation. Little direct evidence has been put forward to show that biotic interactions are major determinants of pond biotic diversity. However, changes in fish populations are often accompanied by changes in the plant and invertebrate communities (Macan, 1965, 1977b; Korinkova, 1967; Henrickson & Oscarson, 1985) and the effect of fish predation on zooplankton community structure is well documented (see Zaret, 1980). Biotic interactions might possibly be a major influence from the very earliest stages of pond colonization. In new ponds, extensive pure stands of emergent or floating-leaved macrophytes may establish within a few years (Barnes, 1983) and preclude other species by competition for light or space. They may constitute very distinctive habitats for invertebrates and if, by chance, different aggressive species colonize neighbouring ponds, then quite different communities may result. (c) Water chemistry. Many workers have found a correlation between pond biotic diversity and water chemistry. Scandinavian studies of molluscan communities (e.g. Aho, 1987a; Økland, 1980) link species diversity to a combination of pH and calcium levels. Strong positive correlations between pH and numbers of species of Crustacea have been reported from acidic, low-calcium ponds and lakes in Northern Britain (Fryer, 1980) and Norway (Økland & Økland, 1980). The composition of macrophytic communities may also be changed during lake acidification (Grahn, 1975). Green (1986) found a non-linear relationship between conductivity and zooplankton diversity in crater lakes. Several authors stress the importance of the general level of productivity of a water body (usually gauged by concentrations of nutrient ions) in determining the assortment of species found there, e.g. Saether (1975). In the present study, the distribution of littoral macroinvertebrates and macrophytes in a group of ponds within a small geographical area were investigated to discover which factors best predict the numbers of taxa and the types of communities found in each pond. In view of the difficulties inherent in distinguishing the confounding effects of different types of variables, the ponds were chosen to minimize the possible influence of pond age and isolation. Sites Sixteen ponds were chosen from among the large number of water bodies created by open-cast extraction of ball-clay in the Isle of Purbeck, Dorset, U.K. The study ponds all lie within an area of heath, woodland and pasture, 5×2 km, centred on National Grid Reference SY935835, just north of the chalk escarpment (Fig. 1). The ponds were chosen to represent as wide a range of physico-chemical and habitat conditions (as judged from terrestrial and aquatic vegetation) as possible. The exact ages of individual ponds are not known, but all date from the nineteenth century, with the exception of pond Q, which was formed in the eighteenth century (English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd, pers. comm.). From a study of the rate of colonization of newly created ball-clay ponds in the area (Barnes, 1983), it appears that the equilibrium number of macroinvertebrate taxa for small ponds is approached within 20 years of the first appearance of the water body. It is expected, therefore, that the ponds chosen for this study have attained the colonization asymptote, at least as far as macroinvertebrates are concerned, and any differences in age between them are not likely to be of importance. Dispersal distances between the ponds are small, the greatest nearest-neighbour distance being <1 km. No discrete source of colonizing propagules is recognizable, there being numerous small water bodies (ball-clay ponds, bomb craters and streams) in the area as well as the Corfe River to the east and the River Stour to the north-west. It is therefore assumed that the source pool of colonists is diffuse, so that no pond is substantially more isolated than any other. All the ponds contain at least 1 m depth of water throughout the year and none is connected, at any time, to any other water body. Methods (i) Morphometry Pond areas and shore lengths were estimated from large-scale maps produced by English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd surveyors. For the larger ponds, maximum depths and basin profiles were obtained from depth measure- FIG. 1. Location of the study site and map of the sixteen ball-clay ponds, labelled A–R. ments taken at 5 m intervals along transects; depths of smaller ponds were measured using a lead line from the bank. (ii) Chemistry Water samples were taken from 20 cm below the surface, 2 m from the shore, away from dense vegetation. All ponds were sampled within 2 h around noon on 12 April 1979 and again on 8 August 1979. Temperature and dissolved oxygen were recorded in situ and samples were analysed the same day by the Wessex Water Authority chemical laboratory, Poole, using standard methods (see Barnes, 1981; for details). For each sample, pH, electrical conductivity, turbidity, total hardness, alkalinity, nitrate, ammonium, orthophosphate, and 5-day B.O.D. were determined. Seven samples were later analysed for calcium and two for total aluminium, using an atomic absorption spectrophotometer at the University of Exeter. (iii) Macrophytes All ponds were surveyed during a 2-week period in August 1979 to determine the total area vegetated, the number of species, and their relative abundance, expressed as cover abundance scores as follows: 1 = 0.1–5% of vegetated area 2 = 6–25% of vegetated area 3 = 26–50% of vegetated area 4 = 51–75% of vegetated area 5 = 76–100% of vegetated area (iv) Macroinvertebrates The macroinvertebrate communities of the shallow littoral were sampled using standard sampling units, each consisting of five separate 2 m sweeps with an F.B.A. pond net (mesh aperture 1 mm). Trials showed that five sweeps obtained at least 85% of the species to be discovered by repeated sweeping within a given weed bed. Pond nets tend to under-sample certain elements of the fauna (see Macan, 1977a, for a critique), and the species lists obtained from one period of sampling will not be complete. However, such samples, taken in a standard manner and within a short space of time, may be used to compare communities between ponds. All sixteen ponds were sampled in a 3-day period in early April 1979. All were sampled with equal intensity, that is the number of sampling units employed in each pond was proportional to the extent of the shallow littoral habitat. An increase in the number of samples as pond size increased was deemed necessary to incorporate the apparent greater diversity of littoral habitats in larger ponds. The shoreline of each pond was divided arbitrarily into 100 m stretches and one sampling unit was taken in each 100 m stretch. The positions of the five individual sweeps in each sampling unit were determined by possibility of access to the water. Identification was taken to species wherever possible, but chironomid larvae were identified only to genus, and some members of other groups could be identified only to family. The relative numerical abundance of taxa were expressed as abundance scores as follows: 1 = present, but a mean of <1 individual per sampling unit 2 = 1–10 individuals per sampling unit 3 = 11–100 individuals per sampling unit 4 = >100 individuals per sampling unit The use of approximately logarithmic abundance categories to some extent overcomes the problem of comparing relative abundance of taxa of very different body size and reduces the dominating effect of seasonal swarms of small individuals. Results Numbers of taxa The numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa and macrophyte species found in each pond are shown in Table 1, together with values for selected physical and chemical parameters. The wide range of all these parameters over the sixteen ponds is apparent: for example, the number of macroinvertebrate taxa ranges from twenty-four to eighty-eight; pH from 3.8 to 7.5; and pond area from 0.023 to 2.0 ha. The total number of macroinvertebrate taxa found was 174 and the total number of macrophyte species thirty-one. The relationships between numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa (INVERTS) and macrophyte species (PLANTS) and physical and chemical characteristics of the ponds were investigated by correlation and regression analyses carried out using the statistical package MINITAB 81.1 (Ryan, 1981). Regression analyses were used to discover which, if any, of the biotic, physical and chemical factors might adequately explain the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa or macrophyte species found in these ponds. Preliminary analyses suggested that regression analysis would not be inappropriate, since the measurement errors in the y-variables (INVERTS or PLANTS) are great relative to those in the x-variables (predictors), and the individual variables are approximately normally distributed. Bivariate plots suggested the need to log-transform INVERTS, PLANTS, area and vegetated area for regression analysis (i.e. LINVERTS, LPLANTS, LAREA, LVAREA); this gave an acceptable degree of homoscedasticity in the residuals (Draper & Smith, 1981). Regression analyses proceeded by using predicator variables in turn, and, for multiple regression, adding them one at a time, using a correlation matrix as a guide and inspecting residuals and coefficients at each stage. The effectiveness of the various regression equations for predicting numbers of taxa in individual ponds was assessed by plotting the number of taxa predicted v. the number observed for each pond ('predicted-y v. observed-y' plots). Points falling above the line of equality indicate an over-estimation by the equation, those below an under-estimation (see Fig. 3). As a first step, Pearson correlation coefficients were computed between all pairs of the fourteen variables given in Table 1, log-transformed as appropriate. Sixteen pairs of observations were used in each case, except those involving calcium, for which only seven pairs could be used. Table 2, the correlation half-matrix, shows a number of distinct patterns: (i) LINVERTS is positively correlated with calcium and pH (\( P < 0.01 \)) and with LPLANTS, alkalinity, and LVAREA (\( P < 0.05 \)). (ii) All pairwise correlations between pH, conductivity, B.O.D., total hardness, alkalinity and calcium are significant at the 1% level. (iii) LAREA and LVAREA are correlated (\( P < 0.05 \)), depth is correlated with LAREA (\( P < 0.01 \)), and LVAREA with LINVERTS (\( P < 0.05 \)) but none of these morphometric variables is correlated with any chemical factor. The composition of the sixteen macroinvertebrate communities were compared by calculating a Jaccard similarity index (\( C_J \)) for each pair of ponds: \[ C_J = j / (a + b - j) \] where \( j \)=number of taxa in common and \( a \) and \( b \)=numbers of taxa in the two ponds (Southwood, 1978). A qualitative index was preferred in view of the very large variance in species abundances. The results are summarized in the similarity half-matrix (Fig. 5a), in which the ponds are arranged in order of pH. A predominance of high Jaccard index values near the diagonal indicates the faunal similarity between most of the ponds adjacent, or close together, in the pH ranking. The faunas of ponds E and R (\( C_J = 0.59 \)) and ponds C and D (\( C_J = 0.52 \)) are the most similar. The matrix can be divided, as shown, to reveal other patterns which are best interpreted by reference to Table 3. (a) There are two main groupings of similar pond faunas, the most acid ponds with pH<5.0 (Q, P, R, J and E) and ponds with pH 5.5–6.8 (C, D, K, B, A, G and M). The former group is distinguished by a complete absence of several major taxonomic groups, as described above, but there is considerable overlap in the distribution of other macroinvertebrates between the two groups of ponds. Pond K is atypical among the ‘C–M’ group in the abundance and diversity of its trichopteran fauna. (b) The faunas of ponds F and L are very dissimilar from those of other ponds of circumneutral pH, principally because of their paucity of taxa (\( C_J \) is heavily influenced by the numbers of taxa). However, the faunas of ponds F and L have some unusual features; for example, L is particularly rich in oligochaetes, and both F and L have Asellus aquaticus (Malacostraca), while the other ponds have A. meridianus. Discussion For the majority of the Purbeck ball-clay ponds considered here, the numbers of littoral macroinvertebrate taxa present are closely predicted by a single environmental variable, namely pH. Below pH 5.5, Mollusca, Malacostraca and Ephemeroptera are completely absent, while other taxa, notably the Trichoptera and Chironomini (Diptera), show a reduction in the numbers of taxa present. These patterns concur well with those reported from Scandinavian acidified lakes and North American dystrophic waters, where Gastropoda, Malacostraca and Ephemeroptera are characteristically absent at low pH (Wetzel, 1975; Økland, 1980; Stenson, 1985). In terms of the identities of taxa present, faunal similarities are greatest between ponds of similar pH (Fig. 5a), which suggests that successful colonization of at least some ponds is restricted to a subset of the total Purbeck species pool by chemical, or associated, factors. Marked faunal differences between acid and circum-neutral ball-clay ponds are apparent from the earliest stages of colonization of new ponds in the Isle of Purbeck (Barnes, 1983) so that differences between acid and circum-neutral 'mature' pond faunas are not the result of successional changes or differential dispersal rates between acid-sensitive and acid-tolerant species. Absence of taxa from ponds of low pH is probably due to a suite of factors, both chemical and biotic, which are directly or indirectly consequential on pH. The adverse effects of high hydrogen ion concentrations per se are exacerbated where calcium concentrations are low and levels of toxic metal ions, notably Al^{3+}, are high (Howells, 1984). The toxic effects of low pH have been demonstrated experimentally for a number of freshwater invertebrate groups, notably Crustacea (e.g. Steigen & Raddum, 1981), Ephemeroptera (Bell, 1971), and some Plecoptera and Trichoptera (Raddum & Steigen, 1981). In the Purbeck ponds, calcium levels are very highly correlated with pH, and although total aluminium levels were not measured systematically, two measurements of 70 \( \mu \)g l^{-1} in pond J and 570 \( \mu \)g l^{-1} in pond Q indicate that some of the acid ponds are probably well within the range of Al^{3+} concentrations known to be toxic to fish (Howells, 1984). The water chemistry in acid ponds E, J, P, Q and R is likely to cause severe physiological stress and prevent completion of the life-cycle in sensitive groups and thus ensure that any incoming propagules of these species cannot colonize. Furthermore, changes in certain biotic elements brought about by physiological stress may so change the habitat as to preclude colonization by species which are not themselves acid-sensitive. Stenson (1985) suggests that a loss of grazers (gastropods) and shredders (malacostracans) may have a major influence on littoral feeding relationships in the acidified Lake Gårdsjön. In the present study the macroinvertebrate faunas of acid ponds are characterized by what is absent, rather than what is present. Few taxa are recognizably 'acidophilic' in their distribution, with the possible exceptions of the chironomid Acamptocladius ?submontanus and the mayfly Leptophlebia marginata. The Odonata also appear to be better represented in ponds of pH<6.8. There is no evidence in these data of the biologically mediated pH effect reported by Hendrikson & Oscarson (1985), namely that loss of fish, the major visual predators, during lake acidification results in increased abundance of large, active invertebrates such as corixids and Notonecta (Hemiptera) and dytiscids (Coleoptera). Fish are absent from most of the ponds below pH 6.5 (A, B, C, D, E, J, P, Q and R), but there is no indication of a greater relative abundance of Hemiptera or Coleoptera in these ponds. This lack of agreement may be because the open water ('limnetic') species included by Hendrikson & Oscarson were not specifically sampled here. Over the wide range of pH represented in the study ponds, then, differences in faunal composition and diversity between the opposite ends of the pH spectrum may be due to a number of factors, probably acting in combina- tion. Many of these are themselves a direct or indirect consequence of hydrogen ion concentration, and pH alone would seem to provide a convenient index of the macroinvertebrate diversity to be expected in a pond. However, spot pH measurements from different water bodies can meaningfully be compared only if all are taken at approximately the same time and in a comparable way, since the pH of a given water body may vary both spatially and temporally, and with different methods of measurement. Although the general character of the macroinvertebrate communities of the Purbeck ponds is set by water chemistry, there is considerable variation in the details of the assemblages, even in ponds of similar pH. In general, ponds which fall within a narrow range of water chemistry, and not affected by any other overwhelmingly influential factor, may be expected to display a considerable diversity of assemblages, each created by a multiplicity of abiotic and biotic factors acting in unique combinations. Two ponds, F and L, clearly do not fit the linear model relating numbers of taxa to pH. Their faunal impoverishment may be linked to the lack of extensive weed beds in both ponds. The paucity of macrophytes may, in turn, be due to a number of factors, such as dense phytoplankton in the summer, supported by high nitrate and phosphate levels (Table 1), unbroken tree-shade round the margins and disturbance of the littoral sediment by bottom-feeding carp and tench. (The latter two points apply equally well to the richly-vegetated pond H, however.) Ponds F and L both have highly organic littoral substrata which support some distinctive faunal elements: pond F, in common with the other woodland ponds H and K, is dominated by shredders (mainly Trichoptera), while pond L, which also receives run-off from a nearby pig-farm, is dominated by organisms typical of organically enriched habitats, such as Tubificidae (Oligochaeta) and Chironomus spp. (Diptera). The number of species of macrophyte found in the Purbeck ponds bears no clear relationship with any of the factors considered. Some of the species distributions are clearly linked with pH: Sphagnum cuspidatum and Juncus bulbosus, in particular, are typical of the acid ponds. Grahn (1975) shows that Sphagnum species rapidly dominate acidified Swedish lakes, and this creates a characteristic biotope for invertebrates quite different from the habitat provided by aquatic angiosperms. The tenuous link observed here between macrophyte assemblages and water chemistry is in sharp contrast to the close relationship known to occur between lake diatom assemblages and pH (e.g. Battarbee, 1984). It remains to ask why such a wide range of pH occurs in the Purbeck ball-clay ponds. Two main sources of possible variation can be identified: local variations in geology, and differences in the land-use and vegetation immediately surrounding the ponds. Ball-clays are themselves chemically inert, but some clay sequences contain pyritic plant remains, which may be oxidized during changes in the water-table and cause acidification. The incidence of acid and neutral ponds is, however, independent of the oxidation state of the clays in this study area. A far greater influence on water chemistry would appear to be the use and vegetation of the surrounding land. The ponds all lie within the Bagshot Beds sandy deposits, which support Calluna heathland over much of the area (Fig. 1). Water passing through these heathland soils is likely to be acidic and low in nutrient ions. Pinus and Rhododendron occur on the sandier soils producing acidic drainage water, while the various species of deciduous

The Environmental Control of Near-Surface Thermoclines in Boreal Lakes Marguerite A. Xenopoulos* and David W. Schindler Department of Biological Sciences, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta, T6G 2E9, Canada ABSTRACT We report on the effect of lake size, water transparency, and wind on the frequency of transient near-surface thermoclines in 39 boreal lakes from the Experimental Lakes Area (ELA) and Northwest Ontario Lake Size Series (NOLSS). This study was based on more than 3000 archived temperature profiles amassed over a 25-year period for lakes ranging from 2 ha to 8 million ha in surface area. The incidence of transient thermoclines decreased with increasing lake size from 90% of all summer days in small lakes (less than 4 ha) to 40% or less in the larger NOLSS lakes (up to 34,700 ha). No transient near-surface thermoclines were detected in Lake Superior. Forest fires and climatic variability were also found to affect the frequency of near-surface thermoclines. Long-term trends indicate an increase in average annual wind velocity in the area, possibly as the result of extensive forest fires and clearcutting. The subsequent decrease in the frequency of shallow secondary thermoclines in aquatic ecosystems has possible consequences for the lake biota, as the result of changes in radiation, turbulence, and the nutrient regime. Key words: near-surface thermoclines; boreal lakes; stratification; interannual variability; forest fires; wind; lake size; lake transparency. INTRODUCTION Thermal stratification influences a wide variety of biological, chemical, and physical processes in lakes, including nutrient cycling, primary production, the depth distribution of organisms, and water movement (Schindler and others 1996a; Sellers and others 1998). Seasonal thermocline depth is influenced by lake size and water clarity (Gorham and Boyce 1989; Mazumder and others 1990; Fee and others 1996). As lake area increases, wind fetch increases and seasonal thermoclines deepen (Arai 1981; Patalas 1984; Fee and others 1996; King and others 1997). Recent studies have shown that changing climatic conditions (Schindler and others 1990, 1996a, b; King and others 1999; Snucins and Gunn 2000) and logging operations (Scully and others 2000; Steedman and Kushneriuk 2000) can also influence thermocline depths in lake ecosystems. In addition to a main seasonal thermocline, near-surface thermoclines (also called “secondary thermoclines”, “transient thermoclines”, or “diurnal thermoclines”) form under sunny and near-windless conditions (Imberger 1985) and can retain the plankton under photoinhibitory irradiances (Vincent and others 1984). Near-surface thermoclines, which can be as shallow as 0.3–1 m, isolate the upper part of the epilimnion for periods of several hours during daylight, but they are usually destroyed by convective mixing at night (Imberger 1985; Imberger and Patterson 1990). Any organisms trapped in the near-surface layer can be exposed to high solar irradiances, including UVB radiation, with attendant effects on their growth and physiological state (Vincent and others 1984; Milot-Roy and Vincent 1994; Xenopoulos and others 2001, forthcoming). Near-surface thermoclines can also influence phytoplankton production and species composition (Lewis and others 1984; Vincent 1990; Frenette and others 1996; Berman and Shteinman 1998; Sherman and others 1998). Phytoplankton in different layers can also have different photoadaptive properties (Falkowski 1983; Lewis and others 1984). Despite their recognized importance to biological processes, to date no study has examined the frequency of transient near-surface thermoclines, and systematic studies of their occurrence are not available. The presence of near-surface thermoclines usually goes unnoticed, although they may effectively isolate the upper epilimnion for several hours, with subsequent effects on many biological processes (for example, UV damage of phytoplankton.) (Xenopoulos and others 2000) and chemical processes (for example, diurnal photobleaching of dissolved organic matter) (Gibson and others 2001). We hypothesized that, like seasonal thermoclines, the formation of near-surface thermoclines would be affected by lake size, water transparency, temperature, and wind. We based our analysis on approximately 25 years of data from nearly 40 lakes spanning several orders of magnitude and a wide range of water transparencies. We show that near-surface thermoclines are unexpectedly common even in large lakes. METHODS Study Site All lakes used in this study are located in the Canadian Shield in northwestern Ontario’s boreal forest and therefore experience similar climate and also have similar topography and vegetation. Twenty-five years of archived temperature data from the Experimental Lakes Area (ELA) (49°40′ N, 93°44′ W) were used initially to detect size-related differences in the frequency of near-surface thermoclines (Table 1). Over the period of study, the ELA experienced climatic warming, with progressively warmer and drier weather during the 1970s and 1980s, resulting in severe forest fires around the ELA watersheds that may have contributed to an increase in wind velocity (Schindler and others 1990, 1996a; France 1997). Forest fires play a major role in determining the distribution of terrestrial plants and animals of this region. It appears that the ELA region is subjected to forest fires, on average, every 50–100 years. To examine the frequency of near-surface thermoclines in larger lakes, we used data from the Northwest Ontario Lake Size Series (NOLSS) study and lakes Superior and Nipigon (Fee and Hecky 1992; Fee and others 1992 (Table 1). The NOLSS lakes are located in the Red Lake District of northwestern Ontario (51° N, 94° W, 150 km north of ELA). Morphometric details of the lakes and the NOLSS study are presented in Fee and Hecky (1992) and Fee and others (1992). A summary of the ELA and NOLSS data is shown in Table 1. Temperature Measurements Temperature profiles of the ELA lakes have been recorded on a regular basis since 1968. Temperature measurements were usually taken during the morning collection of lake water chemistry, generally between 8 AM and noon (Cruikshank 1984, 1988, 1994). Temperature profiles of the ELA lakes were taken weekly or twice monthly for most of the lakes. In the earlier years (1968–80), ELA temperature measurements were taken using a Whitney thermistor with an accuracy of 0.1°C. For all other ELA temperature profiles, a Flett Research Mark II Digital Telethermometer was used (accuracy, 0.1°C) (Flett Research, Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada). All thermistors were calibrated frequently with a National Bureau of Standards mercury thermometer with an accuracy of 0.02°C. Profiles were obtained by starting at the lake surface and taking temperature (T) readings at 1-m intervals. Near-surface thermoclines were deemed to be present when T_{0m}–T_{1m} was at least 0.2°C. Only the period of summer stratification was considered (when surface T was more than 8°C). By inspection, we also eliminated the rare cases where the depth of the main thermocline was less than 1.1 m in our temperature profiles. In 1986 and 1987, temperature measurements from the NOLSS study were made using the Flett thermistor. After 1987, temperature measurements were taken with a free-falling temperature profiler (accuracy, 0.05°C) (R. Brancker, Ltd, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada) that measured temperatures at depth intervals of approximately 0.05 m. For analytical consistency, the same criterion for the presence of near-surface thermoclines was applied as for the ELA data. Although a temperature difference of only 0.02°C is sufficient for near-surface thermoclines to develop (see, for example, Imberger 1985), we decided to use a temperature difference of 0.2°C to describe near-surface thermoclines in this study, given the accuracy of our thermistors (0.05°C and 0.1°C). We also chose to consider only the summer stratification period (mid-May to mid-September, when surface T is more than 8°C), which is the period of highest biological activity. In total, 3344 profiles from 39 ELA and NOLSS lakes were used. The instruments were cross-calibrated to correct for the difference in thermistor sensitivity (accuracy). Temperature profiles were taken simultaneously with both Flett and Brancker thermistors on several occasions during the summer of 1998 in three ELA lakes. A calibration factor was calculated and applied to the ELA data set to facilitate comparisons. Wind Measurements Daily wind velocities were measured with an Atmospheric Environment Service (AES) anemometer and anemograph, type 45B, located at the ELA meteorological site, approximately 350 m west of the shores of Lake 239 (one of the reference lakes at the ELA). Additional details on wind measurements are presented in Beaty (1981, 1984) and Beaty and Lyng (1989). Wind velocities were measured hourly from 1969 to 1994 at 10 m above ground. The wind data reported here are means of the hourly measurements for the ice-free season of each year. Wind at the surface of the lake (field wind data) is available for ELA only after 1990 and was taken at the center of the ELA lakes with a hand-held anemometer (Turbo-meter; Davis Instruments, Hayward, CA, USA) at the same time as the temperature profile (instantaneous measurements at approximately 1-m height). Wind measurements at the surface of the NOLSS lakes are not available. Water Density Calculations The Brünt-Väisälä (N) frequency was calculated as a thermal stability index as in Spigel and Imberger (1987): \[ N = (g / \rho_0 \cdot d\rho / dz)^{1/2}, \] where \( g \) is the acceleration due to gravity, \( \rho_0 \) is the maximum density in the water column, and \( d\rho / dz \) is the vertical density gradient (for 0 m–1 m). Density profiles were calculated for ELA only from temperature measurements when \( T_{0m} \geq T_{1m} \) and \( T_{0m} > 8^\circ \mathrm{C} \). Extinction Coefficient For ELA and NOLSS, extinction coefficients (\( K_d \)) of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) were calculated from the statistical regression of the natural logarithm of light on depth (Fee and others 1991). All \( K_d \) values were averaged for each lake for the whole sampling period. Statistical Analysis The environmental variables (surface area, wind, and \( K_d \)) were tested using linear or, where applicable, nonlinear regressions for their ability to explain the variance in the frequency of near-surface thermoclines. Only the best-fitting models (as determined from \( r^2 \) comparisons) are presented here. The critical probability level was adjusted using the Bonferroni approach to \( \alpha = 0.0025 \), for the relationship between surface area and near-surface thermoclines, for which several nonlinear regressions and transformations were tested. Intercorrelation amongst independent variables negated the possibility of using multiple regression analysis in this study. All regressions were done using JMP (SAS Institute 1996). RESULTS AND DISCUSSION The Influence of Lake Size Near-surface thermoclines occurred on a high proportion of summer days in all lakes, except for Lake Superior. Their incidence decreased with increasing lake size (surface area, \( A_0 \)) (Figure 1). At the ELA, near-surface thermoclines generally occurred on over 40% of all summer days in lakes under 50 ha in surface area. In smaller lakes (approximately 2 ha) the frequency increased to approximately 90% (Figure 1). The much larger NOLSS lakes also showed a high frequency of near-surface thermoclines, ranging from 25% (Nipigon) to about 40% (Musclow, Sydney, and Trout). Near-surface thermoclines, as defined here, were not detected in Lake Superior. The frequency of near-surface thermoclines in boreal lakes declines rapidly with lake area from 2 to 100 ha; it then reaches an asymptote for larger lakes, where near-surface thermoclines occur about one-third of the time during the summer. Although our analysis indicates a strong relationship between occurrence of near-surface thermoclines and lake size, it probably underestimates the actual frequency of occurrence. Near-surface thermoclines can form with temperature differences as small as 0.02°C (Imberger 1985; Shay and Gregg 1986; Imberger and Patterson 1990), and the actual frequency of near-surface thermoclines is probably higher than that calculated in this study. For example, we found that if near-surface thermoclines were calculated from a temperature difference of 0.5°C or greater, the regression curve (in Figure 1) shifts towards the x-axis (frequency is lower) while maintaining the same shape. Water Transparency Some of the variance in the frequency of near-surface thermoclines can be explained by differences among the lakes in degree of light penetration. In clear lakes, solar radiation penetrates farther, distributing heat to a greater depth and causing deeper thermoclines. The incidence of near-surface thermoclines increased with increasing extinction coefficient, \( K_d \) (Figure 2). The depth of main thermoclines is greater in clear-water lakes Figure 1. Frequency of secondary thermoclines in a range of lake sizes in the ELA and NOLSS. The regression is frequency (%) = 17.7/log A_0 + 31.9, \( r^2 = 0.60 \) (\( P < 0.0001 \)). A range of statistical regression lines was tested for their ability to explain the variance in % near-surface thermoclines. The asymptotic regression model above was found to be the best fit (as determined from \( r^2 \) comparisons). Figure 2. The relationship between frequency of near-surface thermoclines (%, \( \Delta T \geq 0.2^\circ \mathrm{C} \)) and light extinction coefficient (\( K_d \)) for the ELA and NOLSS. The regression is: frequency (%) = 32.2 (\( K_d \)) + 26.4; \( r^2 = 0.45 \) (\( P < 0.0001 \)). than in brown-water lakes, independent of lake size (Salonen and others 1984; Pérez-Fuentetaja and others 1999; Snucins and Gunn 2000). Within individual lakes, thermocline depth increases if the water becomes clearer, as is commonly observed during prolonged periods of drought (Schindler and others 1996a; Dillon and Molot 1997). Because of the greater radiation-absorbing capacity of colored waters, heating is restricted to the surface and multiple thermoclines form more readily (Salonen and others 1984). Mazumder and Taylor (1994) showed that water clarity offered a better explanation for thermocline depth in small lakes (less than 12.5 km\(^2\)) than in larger lakes. Fee and others (1996) also showed that the influence of water clarity on thermocline depth diminished as lake size exceeded 500 ha. However, both mixing depth and transparency were positively correlated with lake size. Thus, the correlation between the development of near-surface thermoclines and transparency (\( K_d \)) could simply reflect the underlying relation with lake size that both variables share (\( P < 0.001, r = 0.49 \)). Temperature-related Density Differences Density differences per unit temperature are greater at warm temperatures. This is potentially important because larger lakes are usually colder in the summer than nearby smaller lakes (Fee and Hecky 1992; Fee and others 1992). As expected, average water stability (N) near the surface of the lake decreased with increasing lake size (Figure 3A). The Brünt-Väisälä frequency was also related to water transparency (Figure 3B, \( r^2 = 0.44, P < 0.001 \)). Interannual Patterns Interannual variations in annual means of daily maximum air temperatures and daily mean wind speed might be related to the development of different annual near-surface thermocline patterns. Since 1970, the average air temperature (Schindler and others 1990, 1996a; Fee and others 1996), wind speed (Figure 4A), and water transparency (Figure 4B) in northwestern Ontario have increased. We hypothesized that the increase in wind would reduce the frequency of near-surface thermoclines at the ELA. In the early 1970s, when ELA lakes were surrounded by dense and mature forests (Schindler 1998), the lakes had a high frequency of near-surface thermoclines (Figure 4C, D). Following two major fires (in June 1974 and June 1980) and clearcutting (in the 1970s and early 1980s), which resulted in the partial removal of vegetation in much of the region surrounding ELA, the average wind increased (Figure 4A) and the frequency of near-surface thermoclines decreased (Figures 4C, D). As expected, the frequency of formation of near-surface thermoclines was inversely related to wind speed (\( r^2 = 0.27; P = 0.0071 \)). However, the variance explained by this relationship is low. It is not surprising that wind explained only 27% of the variation, for several reasons. Compared to lake size and water transparency, wind probably Figure 3. (A) The relationship between the average Brünt-Väisälä frequency (N) and lake size for ELA lakes. N was averaged per lake for the years 1968–94. The regression is N = 0.0256 – 0.0088 (log A_0), \( r^2 = 0.39 \) (\( P = 0.0004 \)). (B) The relationship between N and K_d. The regression is N = 0.0081 (K_d) + 0.0108, \( r^2 = 0.34 \) (\( P = 0.0003 \)). has less potential to explain the variability in near-surface thermoclines that we found. In addition, it has recently been shown that only a small fraction (around 3%) of the turbulent energy flux from wind enters the lake (Wüest and others 2000). Furthermore, solar radiation (solar insolation and general heating) is likely a strong driver of the development of near-surface thermoclines (Imberger 1985), regardless of wind velocity. Air temperature has also been increasing in the ELA area (Schindler and others 1996a), and this may offset the wind forcing on the mechanical development/erosion of near-surface thermoclines. Finally, the ELA experienced a drought in the 1980s, causing an increase in water transparency (Figure 4B) and deeper thermoclines (Schindler and others 1996a). It is possible that near-surface thermoclines were also deeper than 1 m. The annual frequency of near-surface thermoclines was positively related with the annual average K_d in Figure 4B (\( P < 0.05; r^2 = 0.22 \)). Clearly, further studies are needed to assess the relative importance of solar radiation, wind, lake size, and lake clarity. It seems that deforestation will only affect stratification patterns (such as thermocline depth) in small lakes (less than 4 ha) (Rask and others 1993; Figure 4. (A) Average wind velocity at the ELA weather station during the ice-free season and linear regression line for the data. (B) Yearly average K_d for all ELA lakes and linear regression line for data. (C) Yearly average frequency of near-surface thermoclines for all lakes during the ice-free season at the ELA. (D) Yearly average frequency of near-surface thermoclines in L239. Asterisks indicate dates of forest fires in the catchment. Two major fires occurred around the L239 watershed. The first, in late June 1974, burned over 50% of the catchment. The second, in June 1980, burned approximately 70% of the catchment. Steedman and Kushneriuk 2000; Scully and others 2000). Recently, Steedman and Kushneriuk (2000) found that logging does not increase wind reaching the surface of lakes 30–40 ha in size. Although wind measured at the ELA weather station has increased since 1970 (Figure 4A), following the fires and clearcutting, it is difficult to assess whether this translated into wind changes at the lake surface. Available field wind data (compiled after 1990) indicate that average wind speeds at the surface of the ELA lakes increase logarithmically with surface area (Figure 5). These data also show that wind speeds at the lakes’ surface quickly reach an upper limit. This upper limit is similar to the average wind velocity measured at the ELA meteorological station for 1990–94. More data are clearly needed to accurately assess the influence of deforestation on wind exposure in lakes of all sizes. CONCLUSIONS The high frequency of near-surface thermoclines indicates that they can be an important determinant of lake biology and chemistry. Williamson and others (1996) showed that near-surface thermoclines occurred 28% of the time in a range of lakes in the northeastern United States. While these lakes were similar in size to the ELA lakes, the lower frequency of near-surface thermoclines reported by Williamson and others (1996) is a result of the criteria (\( \Delta T > 1^\circ \mathrm{C} \)) used in their determination. Here we have demonstrated that the frequency of near-surface thermoclines can be much higher than 28%. Figure 5. Relationship between average wind at the lake surface (1990–94) and lake size for lakes at the ELA. Inset: relationship between average wind speed at the lake surface and lake size for lakes smaller than 80 ha. The darker regression line does not include the outlier L374. Both regression slopes were found to be significantly equal (\( P > 0.05 \); analysis of covariance). The L374 data point is approximately equivalent to the 1990–94 average wind speed at the ELA meteorological station of 11.4 km h\(^{-1}\). In addition to the near-surface layer, which we emphasize here, more attention to deeper substrata seems important. The intensity of UV radiation and photosynthetically active radiation, the intensity of turbulence, and nutrient conditions can differ among sublayers (Spigel and Imberger 1987; Ivey and Imberger 1991; MacIntyre 1993). Small temperature differences within the epilimnion have usually been ignored by chemists and biologists, although they affect many important ecological processes. For example, Xenopoulos and others (2000) found significant changes in the species composition of the algal community when shallow surface thermoclines and high incident UV co-occurred. Weak and transient as these thermoclines are, they are present very frequently and can have important effects on both species assemblages and ecosystem processes in lakes of all sizes.
